prose.en: There comes to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, most vigilant Prelate, something or other from an exhausted breast; whether I should call it a miscarriage or an offspring, I am in doubt: this one thing I know, that if it has any life, it is not owed to me, from whom, already devoted to death, nothing vital could proceed. But that it may live, perhaps the dignity of the subject matter will bring it about, and likewise the authority of the Bard whom I have plundered: for nothing has flowed from the rich vein of Maro that is not worthy of eternal memory. prose.la: Lector quisquis es, siste, in hoc limine paulisper te moror. Quod hîc damus, sacrum est, de spoliis profanorum. Dederunt ipsum ante me multi, sed à se, suisque verbis: ego sic malui alienis. Phrygium efformamus aulæum, pretiosis & variis aliorum telis, viliora rudis ingenij nostri fila interteximus, ne dissutum opus vndique diffluat. Centonem si dixeris, non penitus aberrabis; in quo mirari desine tam nostraesse omnia, quàm ferè nihil. Ac ne, quod aiunt, arenam sine calce afferremus, sparsas Poëtæ principis sententias, iam inter se commodè vinximus, iam verborum nostrorum quodam velut cæmento commisimus. Non poterit homini id ætatis vitio verti, cùm multa dixerit, à se pauca locutum esse: iam enim eorum in albo sum, quibus
prose.en: Reader, whoever you are, halt; I delay you for a little while on this threshold. What we offer here is sacred, from the spoils of the profane. Many have offered the same before me, but from themselves, and in their own words: I have thus preferred to do so in the words of others. We are fashioning a Phrygian tapestry; into the precious and varied webs of others, we have interwoven the cheaper threads of our own unpolished intellect, lest the unstitched work fall apart on all sides. If you call it a cento, you will not be entirely wrong; in which cease to wonder that everything is as much ours as almost nothing is. From us come the invention and the order of things; the verses and half-lines we have mostly drawn from Virgil, that is, from the very fountain of ornate poetry. And lest, as they say, we should bring sand without lime, we have at times conveniently bound together the scattered thoughts of the prince of poets, at times joined them with a sort of cement, as it were, of our own words. It cannot be turned into a fault for a man of that age, though he has said many things, to have spoken few from himself: for I am already on the register of those, to whom

prose.la: Suum enim singulis corymbion fideliter remitto, contentus elegantiæ Virgilianæ, Christianæ fidei, pietatisque solidæ nectar affudisse; vt in ea, velut in artificioso Mentoris scypho, cum literarum ornatu veræ succum religionis inueniat & hauriat Iuuentus studiosa. Quàm nihil sit hoc præstitisse, post intermissa nouem lustris literarum studia, tu dispice. Quamquam enim suaue sit Pimplæis fontibus vuescere, tamen vbi iam annorum frequentia, earum, quæ prima inhæserant iuuentute, rerum obliuionem inuexit, labor hic, vel te iudice,
prose.en: For I faithfully return to each his own hairpiece, content to have poured the nectar of Christian faith and solid piety upon Virgilian elegance; so that in it, as in an artfully crafted cup of Mentor, studious Youth may find and drink the essence of true religion along with the ornament of letters. Consider for yourself how trifling a thing it is to have accomplished this, after literary studies had been interrupted for nine lustres. For although it is sweet to be moistened by the Pimplean springs, nevertheless when the multitude of years has already brought on a forgetfulness of those things which had taken root in early youth, this labor, even in your judgment,

prose.la: Sed amaritudinem hanc detersit planè, quem inde spero, fructus. Nonne enim magnum videri debet, si quæ fidei documenta, soluto sermone, Christiana Iuuentus semel imbiberit, velut saluti necessaria, ea tanti Poëtæ expressa versibus, altiùs inhæreant? Fruere, Lector, & emarcidi iam trunci malum insititium, explicata fronte deliba.
prose.en: But the fruit which I hope for from it has completely wiped away this bitterness. For ought it not to seem a great thing, if those teachings of the faith which Christian Youth has once imbibed in prose, as necessary for salvation, should take deeper root when expressed in the verses of so great a Poet? Enjoy, Reader, and with an unfurrowed brow taste the grafted fruit of a trunk now withered.

prose.la: Georgius Chamberlinus Cathedr. Eccles. Gandauensis Decanus.
prose.en: George Chamberlain, Dean of the Cathedral Church of Ghent.

sentences.en: Well done, old man, from whose clear spring of Maro, its stream now cleansed, the Muse sings sacred things.
Well done again, venerable old man, nourished by a greater spirit within and full of prophetic breath.
You lay open the Latin Bard's poems, which are not empty, and you unlock the unknown songs he gave.
You bring it about that these breezes enliven holy ardours, and that a chaste ember fosters a new flame.
That vein used to flow with a soft whisper and gave only words in a trifling murmur; now it is wise, and, drunk in its mind on better juices, it distils divine nectar and ambrosia.
And although you are changed and wear your accustomed buskins, she is another, and she is the same, under the robe of Bavarius.
Truly, altered from her former dress, she unknowingly foretold the health-bringing work of religion.

And while the prophetic mind, more powerful with uncorrupted frenzy, pours forth divinely inspired words in sacred measures, renowned Rome, conquered, adds to your spoils the illustrious laurels that Mantua won from Apollo.

sentences.en: Here two portents come forth within a single book: a Christ-worshipping Maro, and Apollo made an old man.

You want me to applaud; you want me to tell of unaccustomed things in unaccustomed verse; you want me to become a theologian poet. A greater prodigy is a white-haired poet; but thrice the greatest is Maro, returned from the underworld and now a poet of the heaven-dwellers.
Why should this matter not call for a theologian poet, if Phoebus, once blooming and now a white-haired Apollo, is able and willing to be a Christian, though formerly a pagan?
Age has brought it about that he wills Maro, formerly a pagan, to be a Christian.

sentences.en: What new form covers you, Maro? Did the Samian sage teach you to lay aside your ancient shape?
Or who allowed you to retrace your steps from the Elysian grove? Who opens the empty ivory for you?
Doubtless it is not the gate gleaming with sawn ivory that shows you the way, but the gate of horn that shows you a safe path to the world above.
With a new Mercury leading the way, you escape from here to the upper air, so that after the Countryside, the Leaders and the Pastures you may sing of sacred things.

While the Fathers serve the better first courses at the table, food with which they restore their strength, and set out full cups, pouring not water from a clear spring but wine, it is right for me to indulge the palate of the young with enticements.
Here I renew the feast. For the second course I bring pleasing gifts, and I heap the altars with loaded platters.

marginalia.text_en: A description of the Muse of Maro.
marginalia.explanation: This note labels the portrait that follows. Virgil’s Muse—once the source of Mantua’s pagan poetic glory—is imagined as cleansed by the river of life, worshipping God, and offering honour at Christian altars: a miniature statement of the book’s conversion of Virgil to Catholic use.

sentences.en: With God renewing the strength of body and mind, the old man, serene in mind, has gained the youth of an eagle.
Relying on this, let him dare to vie with the Muses of the young, O seventh one, for whom a decade rolls round in Phoebus' circuit.
Yet in such a way that, in a vigorous, green and flourishing old age, his vein may sound forth nothing but Andine measures.

God's commands are pressing, and so are the sacred lips of the Virgin Mother, who seemed to utter such words as these: "Shall Cypris read her Aeneas in this song, and shall mine flow in simpler verse?
Go now, Muses, and call back your Maro, so that my Son may sound forth from this very mouth."
She spoke, and Maro rises again from the Elysian shores and sings at your command, greatest Virgin.

Death, ripe for an old man, falls headlong, just as damp night falls from the sky, and the setting stars urge sleep. Yet I myself would wish my life to last three days more. Nay, I would wish the last part of my life to remain so long that, returning to my homeland in the company of faithful Achates, † I may lead down with me from the Aonian peak the Muse who once brought you outstanding palms, O Mantua, * near the water where the huge Mincius wanders in slow windings and fringes its banks with tender reeds:

sentences.en: for joys thrill her silent breast, because now, no longer hateful to the Heavenly ones, she draws the breath of life. For she is purified by the wave of the river of life; as a suppliant she adores the divine Godhead and, mindful of her vows, now places her offering on the altars. Indeed, she is preparing to recount what cradles of the faith will pour forth gentle flowers for the Christian people, since no page is more pleasing than one that inscribes the name of faith upon itself. Every grove resounds with the applause and zeal of those who show their favor, the enclosed shores roll the voice along, and the struck hills echo with the shout.
Strew the ground with leaves and cover the grass with foliage, O bards; the Muses command that such things be done for them.
But you, youth of Latium, look upon this part, like certain heavenly gifts of airy honey: marvelous spectacles of slight things for you. Yet it would be a sin to have set serious things below play.
The labor lies in weighty matters, but the glory is not slight for anyone whom the hostile powers permit and whom Jesus hears when called upon.
Behold, the Muse of Maro will give you the answers of faith; here it is lawful for you to hear his very words and to give them back. Be favorable in your minds, and keep your faces intent.

I am she who once played a song on a slender reed, and who, departing from the woods, compelled the neighboring fields to obey the farmer, however greedy he was: a work pleasing to farmers. After this I gave the bristling arms of Mars, and the man who first came from the shores of Troy, exiled by fate, to Italy and the Lavinian shores, much tossed about both on land and on the deep.

But ever since I drank in the laws of Christ with these ears, I have ceased to speak of dire wounds, deaths, and horrid wars, of battle-lines and kings driven by their passions to their deaths, of the Tyrrhenian band and all Hesperia gathered under arms. A greater order of things is born for me; I set in motion a greater work, our cradle of faith.

sentences.en: You know the ancient custom of Ausonia; antiquity is known to you. Tell me: when the fathers' resolve for battle sits fixed, does not the Consul, distinguished by the Quirinal robe and the Gabine cincture, unbar the creaking thresholds?

Or is there need that the Queen herself, gliding down from the sky, should thrust open the lingering gates with her hand, and that, with the hinge turned, heavenly force should burst the bolted doorposts of war?

But with his voice he sweetly sounds the threefold God, the three faces of the Godhead, and with the sign of the cross he sends himself into battle. This funereal sign of the Master's golden-leafed tree, sacred through religion and through the dread of fierce Mars,

has always belonged to the Christ-born race: the sign that the right hand fashions and imprints on the forehead, a forehead worn down by ever more frequent use. This sign calls to battle; then the rest of the youth follows, and the brazen horns blow together in hoarse assent. Ausonia, unroused and immovable before, now burns.
It is more fitting than for someone to have plucked the golden-leafed shoots from the tree (as the vain poets once taught us), so that you may be able to look upon the vaults of heaven,

to direct your steps into the groves where the rich branch of the cross shades the fertile ground, so that you may now be, as it were, equipped with gleaming arms and girded with a weapon against the enemy. For under the auspices of the cross we have hearts brave for war, we have courage, and youth tested in action.
Tell me: in which years of boyhood must the youth, the flower of Latium, whom care for the soul troubles, be instructed?

marginalia.text: Hic duplex insinuatur officium Iustitiæ Christianæ.
marginalia.text_en: Here the twofold duty of Christian Justice is suggested.
marginalia.explanation: The preceding Virgilian maxim joins justice toward other people with reverence toward God; Bavarius presents these as the two duties of Christian justice.

marginalia.text: Per vmbras: quia fides suapte natura obscuritatem includit.
marginalia.text_en: Through the shadows: because faith by its very nature includes obscurity.
marginalia.explanation: The note explains the metaphor in the verse: faith concerns realities that are not yet seen clearly.

marginalia.text: b Catholica fides, non tantùm Scriptura sacra, verùm etiam synceris maiorum nostrorum traditionibus nititur.
marginalia.text_en: b The Catholic faith relies not only on sacred Scripture, but also on the pure traditions of our ancestors.
marginalia.explanation: This is Bavarius’s explicitly Catholic claim that doctrine is transmitted through both Scripture and inherited tradition.

marginalia.text: Traditiones Patrum, sero vsu suo, assimilantur arbori, quæ seminibus iactis, se tandem in altum sustulit, factura seris nepotibus vmbram.
marginalia.text_en: The traditions of the Fathers, by their late use, are likened to a tree, which, after seeds are sown, has at last raised itself on high, about to make shade for late descendants.
marginalia.explanation: The tree is an image of cumulative tradition: planted in the past, it matures slowly and shelters later generations.

sentences.en: What sort of things are the songs that the poet most celebrated for his art, having practised the woodland Muse on a slender reed, recently wrote down on the green bark of a beech tree? They are the things our page will reveal here in a few words: hoary Faith; sure hope of heaven, to which the ardent love of God is joined; and the sevenfold mysteries of the soul's salvation. Be warned, and learn justice and not to despise the gods.
Let the will stand firm in your heart to be duly instructed in these studies, whether the eighth year has not yet taken hold of you, or when first youth clothes your cheeks with its bloom,

Hoary faith is a gift and a distinguished paternal light that protects the people under the ancient religion. It is a star trailing a torch, which has run its course with abundant light, coming to show oracles for fallen affairs and sure oracles for things to come, sent from heaven through the shadows.

He does not plant stumbling footsteps on the trodden ground. Instead, with firm and unmoved faith, having followed the sacred gifts, he holds stored in his mind the more hidden things of our faith, and what the first parents taught in the sacred shrines, whether those things were entrusted to the light leaves of papyrus (which fly scattered, playthings for the swift winds) or handed down of old by the hands of the Fathers to their descendants.
So the tree that has raised itself from scattered seeds grows slowly, destined to give shade to descendants born long after.

marginalia.text: Docemur hîc, dum in dubio est animus, vt in fide Catholica roboremur, non esse vllo modo ad vanas superstitiones recurrendum, sed crebra frequentique oratione, variáque corporis maceratione ad Christum Dominum serio confugiendum, offerendo ei sacrificium Agni immaculati, & cæsarum ouium, sanctorum Martyrum: gestando cilicium, in pellibus caprinis, in melotis noctes ducendo insomnes, vt possimus à Deo visitari, eiusque diuino lumine illustrari.
marginalia.text_en: We are taught here that, while the mind is in doubt, so that we may be strengthened in the Catholic faith, we must in no way resort to vain superstitions, but rather earnestly take refuge in Christ the Lord through frequent and repeated prayer, and various mortifications of the body, offering to him the sacrifice of the immaculate Lamb, and of the slaughtered sheep, the holy Martyrs: wearing a hairshirt, spending sleepless nights in goatskins and sheepskins, so that we may be visited by God, and illuminated by his divine light.
marginalia.explanation: Bavarius rejects pagan divination in the preceding Virgilian lines and supplies a Catholic alternative: prayer, ascetic discipline, Christ’s sacrifice, the martyrs, and monastic penitential dress.

Therefore, troubled by portents, stop consulting the oracles of Faunus, the prophetic Seer, and the groves beneath lofty Albunea, greatest of the woods, which resounds with its sacred spring and, in its shadows, breathes out savage Mephitis.

When in doubt, seek answers here. Here too let the priest bring gifts, and in the silent night let him lie down on the spread fleeces of slaughtered sheep and call for sleep, so that he may hear the heavenly voice, enjoy converse with the gods, and, uncertain where the fates are leading, be able to learn by sure signs where he is granted to settle.

The almighty Father, who holds supreme power over all things, in the beginning founded from nothing the heaven, the lands, the liquid plains, the shining globe of the Moon and the Titanian stars; and a Mind, infused through their limbs, animates the whole mass and mingles itself with the great body. From this come the race of men and beasts, the lives of flying creatures, and the monsters that the sea bears beneath its marble surface.

sentences.en: The Offspring born to God, who rules the affairs of men and gods with eternal commands and terrifies with the thunderbolt, is the one strength of the supreme Father, his own great power: a power equal to God, a force matched equally with the Thunderer.
At length time has brought to us, who longed for it, this help and the coming of God: when first a woman, bearing the face and garb of a virgin, wondrous to tell,
For thus the prophets sang, with an awe-inspiring omen, that a man was coming, proud over peoples and lands, born of heavenly seed, who would seize the world by his might.

And now the promised day was at hand, the time when the origin of the divine lineage, sent under command, first raised his sacred face; and power mingled with God came forth from the body, and the image of the dear Father appeared.

So the Prophet begins, with the Sibyls as his witnesses: "The last age of the Cumaean song has now come. Now the Virgin too returns, and the Saturnian kingdoms return. A royal progeny is sent down from high heaven, offspring of the eternal Godhead, through whom the iron race first ceased, and a golden race will arise throughout the whole world. Chaste Lucina, show your favour: my Jesus now reigns."

O Mary, God himself made you a parent of this fair offspring. With the fruitful showers of the holy breath he descended into the lap of the joyful Virgin, and the Great One, mingled with the holy body, nourishes the lofty offspring.

sentences.en: Meanwhile you, destined to resemble God the Father in face and shoulders, remain an undefiled virgin. The offspring himself gives you beautiful flowing hair and the radiant light of youth, and he had breathed joyful graces upon your eyes.
The very cradle pours forth charming flowers for you. The serpent perishes too, and the deceitful poisonous herb perishes, and Assyrian amomum will spring up everywhere.
"Run on, such ages," said the Parcae to their spindles, in accord with the steadfast will of destiny.

The Radiance of the high heavens kept himself shut away at home. The royal offspring, the Ruler of highest Olympus, submissive to a parent for so long, chose to bow his neck to the yoke and to live without glory before the whole world, until at last, driven by heavenly commands, he came forth into public view. No one was more excellent than he at rousing men with his speech and kindling minds with his word, and he came forth so that he might cure wounded hearts with healing words, just as the one who was able to spread sleep, by song and by hand, over the viper brood and the heavily breathing water-snakes might soothe their rage and relieve their bites with his mouth.

But he could not heal the blow of envy's spear, and neither sleep-bringing songs nor herbs sought in the Marsian mountains helped them against their wounds. The ungrateful offspring of the Solymi perished in their hatreds; with various rumors they sharpen their anger against the physician and urge that he be bound to a high beam by a hideous kind of death. Alas, pierced in his arms and the soles of his feet, and even with his temples bound in a thorny band, he falls as a slain victim, a priest celebrating new sacred rites, reddening and unadorned. Thus the grape hung on the briars, and the hard oaks sweated dewy honey.
By this death, if any traces of our sin remain, they will be rendered void and will free the lands from perpetual fear.
Meanwhile the nourishing Parent could not bear that the lifeless body, pierced through the breast, should be left without the honor of a tomb.

sentences.en: They make ready, and they wash and anoint the body of the cold one. A groan arises; then they lay the limbs they have wept over on a bier and cast purple garments over them, the familiar coverings. Some took up the huge bier, a sad service; and here heaped-up Sabaean incense is sought for God. Finally the corpse is veiled. Soon, laid to rest in a hewn rock and not in cheap earth, he is buried by the holy ones, to whom fragrance is dear, to join sweating balsams to the scented wood.

Holy love conquered the harsh journey and drove him to seek the realms unlovely to the living, and to break the brazen gates by his command, when he wished to lead forth the souls of the Saints from the dark cave of the prison and from the lake of Cocytus.

Soon the cave and the vast palace of Limbo appeared uncovered, and the shadowy caverns lay open deep within. It was just as if the earth, gaping utterly open under some force, should unlock the infernal dwellings and reveal the pale realms hated by the gods, and the immense abyss should be seen from above, and the shades should tremble at the light let in.

Scarcely had the third Dawn brought back her saffron risings when, retracing his steps, he returned to the upper air. Then suddenly, before their eyes, the tomb of immense bulk, where the lifeless body had been laid: neither its barriers nor the guards themselves are able to hold out. They see rocks torn from rocks, and the tight joints of the sides loosened. A sound arises, and the earth is shaken by a massive weight.

sentences.en: On the fortieth day he parts the breathing shadows through the yielding air and, borne along in the open sky, left mortal sight in the middle of his speech. Enclosed in a cloud (marvelous to tell), he brings himself in, and the glory of the starry heaven receives him on a throne and holds an eternal name through the ages.

And at last, as the years glide by, an age will come when he will appear in the full majesty of the Thunderer, seated on a high throne and girt with the gleaming arms of the winged ones, so that as Judge he may dispense justice, ready to give to each according to what his own virtue and life have earned. Trojan and Tyrian alike will be treated by him without distinction.
Just as the affairs of men and of gods, and the whole world which he founded, the almighty Father, with the Offspring coeval with his parent,

rules with eternal commands, and all things far and wide on every side, beyond the paths of the year and the sun, where heaven-bearing Atlas turns on his shoulder the axis studded with burning stars; so, in the same way, the breathable Deity, sent forth to the lands and not unequal in any step to the eternal Father, has extended his empire. And as all adore his deity and load his altars with various gifts, let me therefore match him with the Begetter in equal praise.

I believe in one God, and at the same time in three faces of the Deity. There is the almighty Father, who holds the highest power over all things. The royal Offspring gathers himself to the side of the Begetter. And from both, from the flowing Deity, there issues its own Deity, to whom belong radiance and glory, splendor, and an equal peak of honor.

As much as Rome has raised its head among other cities, and as much as cypresses are wont to rise among the pliant viburnums, so much does the form of the sacred flock whose name is the Church raise its head to the world above the other sheepfolds of men, a flock that extends its empire to the Ocean and its fame to the stars.

sentences.en: She rules with her command the peoples, mothers and men alike; and as Mother she pities spirits long sluggish and hearts grown unaccustomed, and the idle who do not know the way, demanding back that all things be turned and ruled under Christ.

How fortunate beyond measure, if only they knew their own blessings, are the Romans, lords of the world, and the toga-clad nations, the ancient Ausonians! To all of them God also granted that there should be one city for the heavenly ones and for those departed from the earth, that men should hold the gate at a common post, and that they should call upon a common God who is willing to give wine!

For them it is lawful that peoples be mingled and covenants joined between the dwellers in heaven and us who feed on the ethereal air, and among those already laid to rest in the earth, whom they call shades and thin lives without a body.
However things fall out, there is one common danger and one salvation for the peoples joined by this alliance.

Christ himself, of surpassing form, moves among the foremost, holding arms, and stands a whole body above them. A cloud of winged ones follows, and shielded columns are massed across all the plains. A drawn line of steel stands in flashing light, and finally it is certain that battle is joined on every side, on earth and in the sky, with the weapons of vows.

sentences.en: But those deprived of the light of life are not without aids of their own. Besides the funeral offerings that the pious race of Christians destines for the Shades, there are also the sacred words of those who pray, or the prayers of the funeral rite, and gifts given to the needy; cruel scourges, hunger and harsh fasts on behalf of the fallen, a varied kind of penance, and nameless penalties. By these, while the wrath in heavenly minds subsides, they soon empty of their shades the banks that seethe with pitch and black whirlpools, and snatch the souls from the Acherontian flame and from dreadful punishments; and the supreme piety of the highest Parent grants that they be placed in heaven.
So come, pious nation, cease from fear and dismiss your sad dread, you whom cruel horror first surrounded: the city will be bereft of fear when the world has come into the city.

I believe that orders are given for the gates of Cocytus to be closed with iron and tight joints, once the stain is forgiven, by the power of those above, through the ministering key bestowed on Peter.
Let the wickedness of Erebus cease; let impious Frenzy within, sitting on cruel arms and bound behind his back with a hundred brazen knots, roar, horrid with bloody mouth.

Once the earth, shaken by a harsh-sounding tremor, resounded with a groan and, roused, with its tombs torn open, sent forth phantoms. But this condition was given to few; to few was it granted to return to the light of life. Yet there will be a time when the heavenly trumpet will shake the world with its hoarse bellowing, and when all bodies will suddenly rise far and wide through all lands. Then you will see these very things returned to their old shape.
Look at the world nodding under its convex weight: the lands, the tracts of the sea, and the deep sky. Look how all things rejoice in the age to come.

sentences.en: Then wars will be laid aside and the harsh ages will grow mild. No longer will the trumpet give out its terrible sound from sonorous bronze. Instead the rewards of eternal life will be rendered, where there is deep peace, supreme rest, and the joys of heaven.
The Ruler of Olympus will give an empire without end, and he will set no bounds of space or limits of time for his own.

It designates a large assembly of the Christ-worshipping race, which adores the Divinity of Christ. This race is joined by the covenant of faith, is guided by the commands of the divine ones, and is divided across the great world by vast tracts of land. Concerning it the Prophets once wrote that it would be a nation outstanding in war and of easy livelihood through the ages.

To her an outstanding Shepherd is given by divine gift: the supreme one who by dying restored the state to the lands, the hope of the heavenly flock, to whom he has granted the citadels on high. It belongs to his office to impose custom upon peace, to spare the subjected, and to vanquish the proud.
Rightly he will always be a God to me, and a tender lamb from our sheepfolds will often stain his altar.
Happy too are those whom the first after him feeds, the one to whom God thunders with his own mouth that He has handed His own office over to him.
You, Roman Shepherd, remember to rule this flock, feeding them in empty glades and along full rivers, where there is moss and a bank most green with grass.

Do not let the care of dogs be your last concern; feed the swift hounds of Sparta together with the fierce Molossian on rich whey. With those as guards you will never dread the thief in the stables at night, the attacks of wolves, or the unpacified Iberians at your back.

marginalia.text: Saltibus in vacuis ieiunij & abstinentiæ, inueniunt oues Christi pinguia pascua: iisdem sunt plena flumina aquæ salientis in vitam aternam, de fontibus Saluatoris. Hic muscum intelligo alterius generis, quàm sit is qui vel è terra, vel ab animantibus producitur, sed inodorem suauitatis, à fama boni nominis procedit. Viridissima gramine ripa, est repagulum castitatis. Speluncæq; tegant Monachos & Anachoretas, sub umbra alarum Christi Domini, qua ob defensionis robur, saxea dici potest. Per canes, & Spartæ catulos acremque molossum concionatores intellige, quos sero pingui sacræ doctrinæ, à Sede Apostolica conuenit imbui, vt alios doceant, quæ prosint ad salutem.
marginalia.text_en: In the empty glades of fasting and abstinence, the sheep of Christ find rich pastures; there too the rivers are full of water springing up into eternal life, from the fountains of the Saviour. Here by 'muscus' I understand something of another kind than that which is produced either from the earth or from animals: rather, an odor of sweetness, which proceeds from the fame of a good name. The bank greenest with grass is the barrier of chastity. And let caves shelter Monks and Anchorites under the shadow of the wings of Christ the Lord, which, because of the strength of its defense, may be called rocky. By the dogs, the whelps of Sparta, and the fierce Molossian, understand preachers, who ought to be steeped by the Apostolic See in the rich whey of sacred doctrine, so that they may teach others what is profitable for salvation.
marginalia.explanation: Bavarius allegorizes Virgil’s pastoral landscape as Christian ascetic life. Pasture and water become spiritual nourishment; caves shelter monks; fragrance signifies reputation; and Virgil’s dogs become preachers trained in Catholic doctrine under the authority of the Apostolic See.

sentences.en: One must obey the orders and commands of God. To feed his sheep and lambs, your greatest care: let that be your labor, for this is the certain will of the Lord. Obey the command joyfully, and the endeavours of your faith, which it holds established, will remain unmoved.

Provision will not be sufficiently made for the flock and for the flock's master unless the people of God shake off sleep and resolve to keep watch. Keep watch in haste, men; a snake lies hidden in the grass. For the saints, let this fixed resolve to keep watch stand firm in the mind.

Rise, come, let the way be made by force. Relentless toil conquers all. Stir up wars, and let your next care be to set troops in the midst against the wolves, so that they do not join the camps of the sheep.

For it is just as when a wolf lies in ambush against a full sheepfold, growling at the pens past midnight after enduring winds and rains. The lambs, safe under their mothers, keep up their bleating, while he, fierce and relentless in his wrath, rages against those out of his reach. The ravening frenzy to feed, gathered over a long time, wears him out, and so do his jaws, dry of blood.

It is no different when the Furies of Erebus see the closed thresholds of this flock (and the sheepfolds are a care to the Shepherd): their wrath kindles, and pain burns in their hard bones, as they ask by what method they might attempt an approach, and by what way they might shake the enclosed lambs out of the stable and pour them out through the fields.

sentences.en: ...the busy bees, when they fill the honey with sweet nectar. In the same way I must keep far from the sheepfolds of the Lamb the faithless race of Solyma, the Gentile, and the shipwrecked crowd of an abandoned faith, a crowd from which the light has been entirely taken away. Then there are those infected with the heretical plague, who seem to follow our camp while they boast of a great name. Meanwhile the flooding error of a blind mind lies hidden. They nourish wounds in their veins, and they do not open them without war.
But they would far sooner fall to a cruel fate than revoke their false faith, or tame by admonition the monsters of profane perfidy and their own proud arrogance.

There are some who tear themselves completely away from the body itself, like the brothers who conspired to tear down heaven and tried to thrust Jove down from the realms above, when in their savagery they sought to drive the Master of the flock from his seat. So they willingly left the stables, cut off from the rest, with the common peace thrown aside.

A fierce crowd of wicked men gathers at their side. Heavy impiety, conscious of wicked guilt, like some stormy Orion rising with the flood, has carried them into blind shallows. Far out, driven by insolent south winds, through the waves as the sea overwhelmed them and through impassable rocks, it has scattered them onto the Scylla of avenging censure. These unjust men, snatched far away from the folds and sheepfolds of the kindly Shepherd, call in vain on the gods above in their prayers and use the accustomed altars of divine worship.

And, as is their custom, they strive to recline at the tables of the gods and, in vain, to rejoice in the merits of the pious, merits they sought for themselves, together with the common words of those who pray. For, excluded, they are stripped of these just laws. Such is the power the Most High has granted to man.

sentences.en: This I ask of you, a thing bound by no law of fate. I entreat you for Latium, for the majesty of the Thunderer: do not let the native Latins change their ancient name, or become heretics, or be called schismatics, or let the men change their speech or alter their dress. Let Latium endure, let there be Alban kings through the ages, and let the Roman race be powerful by the virtue of Christ, if no nation has celebrated your honors as it has.

Let the Sect fall, and grant that it has fallen, and Schism with it, so that the evil contagion of a neighboring flock may do no harm and the marsh may not cover the pastures with muddy rushes. For unaccustomed fodder would afflict the heavy young.
Let the plagues subside, and, adding the custom and rites of sacred worship, may you make all Latins of one voice.
Nourishing Parent of all things, if any prayers can move you, look upon us, only this. And if our piety deserves it, then grant your help, Father, and confirm all these things.

The Teucrians had exchanged shields and had already fitted the insignia of the Danaans to themselves as the walls of Troy were falling. But suddenly the Danaans recognize the deceit and the false weapons, and notice that their speech sounds different.
Thus, suppose a wolf, changed in his spoils and his face and clothed in the woolly fleece of a sheep, should fill everything around with horrific howls in the manner of a beast.
It belongs to the spirit of Christians, whether of the faith or of their ancestral stock, to proclaim the highest honors to the Supreme Pontiff.

(Just as it belongs to faith itself to come to the help of doubtful matters,) it belongs also that ambiguous matters be resolved at the same time by a fatherly voice, so that faith may be certain: that the Fathers have come together by a divine mind, in harmony through the stable power of the fates, not ignorant of the sacred law, Fathers to whom an inspired ardor came and granted them to go to the stars with uplifted face.

sentences.en: They say that the see, sacred by religion under the Roman name, deserved by the honor of praise to be raised to the stars. God enriched her with the exceptional gifts of the divine breath, and has protected her ever since her very beginning. They want whatever she teaches to be held as having weight, since she is a column resting on God as on firm and solid adamant, which no force of men could destroy in war, nor the Tartarean troops themselves, nor a thousand phalanxes.
Do not seek, I pray, to be taught what fates await these men, and what death will one day engulf the guilty in a burning tomb, with God as witness, those who deceive the wishes of so great a parent.
Should the Prophetess not be to you the surest messenger of truth, she to whom God Himself wished to entrust His own thoughts?

Cease, fool, to hope that God is swayed by praying, so that you yourself may enjoy the embraces of God the Father, while you are turned away from this prophetic Seer, for whom the fates set for her by her spouse will remain unmoved, and whose promises will by no means be torn away. What opinion has turned you, while such great weariness of your pious mother has seized you?
Is this the reward of piety? Is this how you wish to be restored to the sceptre? You are deceived, O race hateful to God, ignorant of the truth.

But rewards worthy of your deeds will be paid back to you, unless your hard heart melts like soft wax. For this honor of mortal life, this very one, which the skillful tending of crops and flocks had barely forged for you as you tried everything, you will leave behind along with your mother, and the Father will not be gentle to you but an unjust stepmother.

Look, he is already making good his words: by God's will they lay down the fierce hearts of the sea, and the land of Holland takes on a spirit at peace with the Latins and a kindly mind, turning its counsel to the better, and at last it will cherish the Romans, lords of the world, the toga-clad race.

It is like a rich field on which golden Ceres, never offended in her godhead, never looks down in vain from high Olympus. It is a joyful field: in no tillage does Moesia boast of herself so much, nor Gargara, which marvels at its own harvests.

sentences.en: And just as the man who breaks up the sluggish clods with mattocks and drags the wicker hurdles helps the farmer's fields, and so does the man who, once the plain has been broken up, cuts back across the ridges he has raised with his plough turned crosswise, and works the earth constantly and lords it over the fields, so God, while he allows this field of his, of rich earth, to be worked by the rakes of swords and by the dark hatreds of tyrants, and to be carried off by violent death, adorns it with more splendid cultivation. We marvel at the ears of grain heavy with manifold yield. What harvests the plains return from a richer bosom, and with what interest!
Unless a grain of wheat dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.

It is a virtue by which God speaks in this way, with a calm voice, to heavenly minds that have a confidence in the kingdom infused from heaven and the soul's sure hope of salvation: "O companions, for we are no strangers to hardship before now, O you who have suffered worse, God will give an end to these things too."

"You have come near Scylla's fury and her deep-resounding crags; you have also known the rocks of the Cyclopes. Call back your courage and put away sorrowful fear; perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember even these things."

"Through various misfortunes, through so many perils, we make our way toward our homeland, where the fates show us quiet dwelling places; there it is right to take up the scepters of the kingdom again. Hold out, and save yourselves for better times, so that this anchor of the homeland may hold you fast with its hooked bite."
Press on, burning for the work: some to build walls, to construct a citadel, and to roll up rocks with their hands; others to prepare a site for a dwelling and to enclose it with a trench.

sentences.en: Just as toil keeps the bees busy beneath the sun through the flowery countryside in early summer, when they lead out the grown offspring of their race, or when they pack the liquid honey and swell the cells with sweet nectar, or receive the loads of those arriving, or form a column and drive the drones, a lazy herd, from the hives.

Kindly Parent of all things, who fill heaven with your divine presence, may your honour, your name, and the praises of your people always resound far and wide through all the mouths of men around the towns, just as the pathless thickets resound with tuneful birds. May very many temples rise to you, and may a thousand altars grow warm for you with Sabaean incense and breathe with fresh garlands.
We are your offspring, to whom you grant the citadel of heaven: bring us back and restore us to the sceptres of the empire we lost.
Just as in heaven, so on earth may your sure will stand unmoved by its own fates, to be heaped with triumphs.
May no Dawn bring her rising here for us without supplying the pleasing gifts of Ceres, won by toil.

The eternal Creator, whom the stars of heaven obey, dwells with you as your offspring. He hides himself in that breast of yours while he resolves to refute the common charge by an infamous death; this remains stored deep in his mind. For your Son has made these covenants with himself for you.

sentences.en: When you are beheld, kindly one, the brightest lights among mothers are darkness. Whatever glory of womanly praise exists anywhere, and whatever belongs to my own lot, falls short of your honours. By this one labour of birth you have embraced countless descendants: all the dwellers in heaven, all who hold the lofty heights above.
And blessed are the offspring of your fruitful childbearing, the fruit of a virgin womb, heavenly gifts, the one salvation for the vanquished, the hope bestowed: gentle Jesus.

Supreme parent of the heavenly ones, we, the guilty, call upon you in our prayers. Since things proceed by a mother's gentle nod, may it not displease you to win by your entreaty peace for your own and the promised kingdoms. Otherwise the black day may carry us off by an ill-omened death, deprived of sweet life, and plunge us into bitter death.

I am she who is the Queen and glory of the virtues. Like a gentle flame kindling the marrow of my soul, I nourish a wound in my veins and am scorched by a hidden heat whenever the image of my dear Father comes to mind. The great virtue of God keeps returning to my mind, and the great honour of his praise. His face and his words cling fixed in my breast, and care grants my limbs no peaceful rest.

While this silent wound lives beneath my breast, none of the mockeries of the vain world delight me at all, since I deem nothing great that does not equal you, O Godhead. You are my life, my father, my mother, my brother and my sister, my bridegroom strong in love; you are the nourisher of the holy heart, giving the sacred cakes of salvation made from wrought Ceres, and giving the thirsting soul the gifts of heavenly Lyaeus.

sentences.en: What you allow me to will, grant by your divine will that I may be able to merit. Grant that I may more fully recognize the traces of the old flame, and may the gratitude for so great a deed stand firm in one who remembers it. May I know neither sweet children nor the rewards of Venus; may I only be the daughter of so great a Father, to be joined in the triumphs of the heavenly fatherland, destined to come beneath the vault of the gods above, while it stays settled in my mind to meet a heavier fate, O God, before I violate you and break your laws.
No: for your loving kindness entered into these covenants with me and gave hope to my doubting mind, and your will has not changed.

I have another care, as our order demands, for this is my labor: to run to the aid of my companions' affairs. I do this so that your offspring, whom you demand for the Olympus of heaven and who is tossed about so much on every side, on land and on the deep, may not pierce the ribs of the soul with mortal sin, and so collapse and at last fall from the heavenly fields.
To me is given the power to kindle hearts with flames, by which they may duly pay their dues to God the Parent.
It does no good to have held out against it two thousand Camilli, swift with the javelin and far superior to the rest in skill.

Grant, Almighty Father, that this disgrace may be wiped out by our arms. I do not seek the spoils or the trophy of heresy driven back, or any booty. Let other deeds bring you praise. So long as this dire plague falls, driven back by my wound, I shall return without glory to my native home.
Come then, great Parent, grant at the very least that part of this vow may succeed, so that the hostile force may not draw near, and so that it may seem to us far more worthy of a triumph.

sentences.en: These two commandments above all were brought down through the swift air by the Messenger of the gods, sent by the Father on high.

Let your mind be wounded by this one sweet care. Let it nourish this one wound in its veins and in the deepest recess of the heart. Then the ardor of the divine Godhead may grow without limit, driving its flames on and gathering strength as it goes. The hiding places of the soul may be laid open and its heat fly up to the air, with its heart on fire, turning over nothing else within itself than duly to pay God the Father his rightful dues. By this path let us hasten to Christ with wondrous love.

Three times I pray that the exalted Mother of God may win for me by her entreaty this great fire in my bones and inflame my kindled soul with a greater love. And so that my foolish mind may not resist her, may she grant that I recognize more fully the traces of the old flame.

Scarcely were these words spoken when the Virgin, her snowy arms about him on either side, cherished the one who prayed in a soft embrace. Suddenly he received the accustomed flame, and the familiar heat entered his marrow and ran through his melting bones, just as sometimes a fiery crack, split open by flashing thunder, runs gleaming through the storm-clouds with its light.

sentences.en: Nisus, following great-hearted Aeneas and the utmost fame, did not shun his companion Euryalus while he threw himself into battle, but sought to join him to his greatest deeds. In the same way, you profane goads of envy, go far from us. Let the unhappy man fear the Furies and the harsh river of Cocytus, the twisting circles of Ixion, the monstrous wheel, and the stone that cannot be overcome. Let this plague be banished from the mind, O best Father of all things. Let no glory be sought for my deeds without you, and grant that I may embrace my companions with a love equal to my own.
That fiery vigor by which we burn supremely for the friendly Deity is a kind of heavenly origin of the soul.

By this the faithful love of children towards the Deities reveals itself; this one thing, I say, is the sure sign: that they carry out the commands. For this is what the very Wisdom of the highest Father teaches.
He who keeps my words and fulfills the commands of the parent bears witness to his true love for me.

If the heat of the eternal Deity has kindled any flaming force among companions, that force is accustomed to produce various effects in the mind, as the Apostle clearly declares in these words: The fiery force among brothers is patient, and kind even to the harsh. It disregards its own and does not envy another's praise. It shudders at wicked things, and it does not let itself be swollen and puffed up with pride. By repressing proud minds, it holds the sceptre, softens hearts, and calms angers. It represses the untamed movements of the mind under the ruling command of the Thunderer, curbing them with chains and a prison:

sentences.en: No fickle ambition and no glory steeped in false paint sits in its heart; nothing vain lingers in this seat. Being gentle, it does not rashly flare up into heavy anger, and it never turns over anything wicked in its heart concerning its companions. It despises all wickedness and is mindful of right and wrong, and that God is the avenger, just as he will bring the just worthy, immortal rewards when the final line of life has come. Moreover, it is devoted to the pursuit of true honour. With heavenly strength, and joyful in mind, she endures the weapons of hostile fortune, the madness of the winds and the roaring storms; indeed, she bears every hardship:
Even though at times she may be sick with immense cares, she puts on a look of hope and represses deep sorrow in her heart, turning over immense courage in her narrow breast.
It is good to state more fully what was said more concisely before, so that the obscure matter may become clear.

The Almighty Father, whom the stars of heaven obey, sent down ten golden commands from high Olympus, with the heavenly trumpet blaring and clarions sounding. "Overcome this yoke," he says; "it is my fixed will for you. Obey the command joyfully, for you will be glad to have fulfilled it." He orders Moses to bring these mandates to the ears of the people.

With such words the Almighty, who holds supreme power over all things, begins. As he speaks, the lofty house of the gods falls silent, the earth is shaken from its foundations, and the lofty ether is silent. Then the Zephyrs settled, and the sea stilled its placid waters.

I myself am the Lord, the Ruler of great Olympus. You shall by no means worship alien things, fashioning divine powers of gods for yourself; let your right hand not form images of false gods. For the deadly gift of unwed Minerva will harm the Trojans less, when Troy falls from its height and its walls are overthrown, than the Mulciber of the golden calf will have harmed the Solymi. Stored deep in the mind there remains the judgment of the Israelite, and the affront of the spurned worship of the eternal name, and then of the ancestral religion.

marginalia.text: Indulgendum putaui neophytae Musae Maronis, vt ad singula Dei praecepta, gentis suae profana citet exempla,cum huius instituti mei ratio postulet, vt eum more suo loquentem,quoad eius fieri possit,audiamus.
marginalia.text_en: I thought indulgence should be granted to the neophyte Muse of Maro, so that at each of God's commandments she might cite profane examples of her own race, since the rationale of this my design demands that we hear him speaking in his own manner, as far as it can be done.
marginalia.explanation: Bavarius licenses his novice Muse to use pagan examples under each commandment because speaking in Maro’s own idiom is part of the cento’s declared method.

sentences.en: No one may lawfully swear by my Godhead and so deceive it. That ancient race of Earth, the Titan brood, did not get away with it unpunished: they soon felt the Godhead's wrath, and, cast down by the thunderbolt, they are rolled about in the lowest abyss.

Behold Salmoneus paying cruel penalties while he tries to deceive the mind that cannot be deceived; while, having imitated the flames of the gods above and the sounds of Olympus, he went about exulting and demanded for himself the honor of the gods, the madman, when the storm-clouds and the inimitable thunderbolt

he would simulate with bronze and the running of horn-hoofed horses. But the almighty Father hurled his weapon from among the thick clouds (no firebrands for him, no smoky torchlight) and drove him headlong in a dreadful whirlwind.
So I would wish everyone to remember that it is not to be borne unpunished: the supreme name, which you can equal with no other in praise,

This is the Father's command, which it is wicked not to obey. With such friendly words he addresses his offspring: "My progeny, let the seventh day be your care, and celebrate all the festivals with goodwill and pious devotion, the annual ones too, which it is a sin to postpone, proclaimed to the world as if from a mother's mouth. For it was not some vain superstition, ignorant of false gods, that imposed these solemnities on you; rather, you keep them as people instructed by the warnings and the Godhead of the gods, and you renew honors that are deserved."

sentences.en: Not as once the Arcadian king brought undeserved honors to Amphitryon's son, a boxer and unworthy of them, in a grove before the city. With him his son Pallas, and together with them all the foremost of the youth and the poor senate, were offering incense, and warm blood smoked at the altars.
Then chosen youths and the priest of the altar eagerly bring the roasted flesh of bulls, load baskets with the gifts of hard-won Ceres, and serve Bacchus.

Let these things be far from ours; go far away, you profane rites. Let the Thyiad be far from here, roused by the shaking of the sacred emblems, when at the sound of Bacchus the triennial orgies spur her on and Cithaeron calls with its shouting in the night.

Let us not allow even the slightest mark to be branded on the sacred rites of the Christians; rather, let them be worthy of God and pleasing to the saints, and let nothing disgraceful touch our altars.

Let the festal day be veiled with festal foliage throughout the city. Let the people devoted to God fill the august, huge temple, lofty with its hundred columns, with the immense zeal of ancestral piety, and let them heap the altars with gifts.

By God's command, let this resolve of a renewed mind be fixed in the offspring: to bring aid to their father's house, to relieve the family with help, to add strength to one who has been overcome, to help with money and resources, which will be a duty of piety, and to expose their heads to heavy dangers for their own.

Thus Aeneas once, following the laws of piety and longing to carry his father out of the flames of Troy, speaks these words as he makes his way through weapons and through enemies: "Come then, dear father, place yourself on my neck; I will carry you on my own shoulders, and this labour will not weigh me down.

However things turn out, there will be one common peril and one salvation for us both. Let little Iulus be my companion, and let my wife follow my footsteps at a distance. You, father, take the sacred objects and our ancestral household gods in your hand.

sentences.en: Having said this, his broad shoulders and bowed neck covered over with a garment and the skin of a tawny lion, he goes beneath the burden, and little Iulus to his right hand
clings, and follows his father with unequal steps; his wife comes up behind, hurrying through the darkest places.

No one may lawfully take a life with cruel steel. The exception is the judge, the avenger of wicked crime and champion of justice, who has been given full power to remove the guilty from our midst by a violent death.

Hence the man who has dared to overcome an unwary companion secretly with the sword shall fall before his day and lie unburied in the middle of the sand, so that his offenses are atoned for by no like punishment.
And although the crimes themselves can be hidden for a long time, it nevertheless happens that hidden wickedness cannot be kept secret forever.

Pygmalion, more monstrous in wickedness than all others, kept up many pretenses for a long time and deceived his sister with wondrous art. But in her sleep the very ghost of her unburied husband came to her, lifting his pale face in wondrous ways. He laid bare the cruel altars and his breast pierced with steel, and uncovered all the hidden wickedness of the house.

In the same way the murder of Polydorus was also betrayed by portents, and the impiety of the Thracian king, twice and three times unspeakable, was made known, along with the hunger for gold that destroys the innocent one.

Shall I speak out, or shall I keep silent? A tearful groan is heard from the depths of the mound, and a voice comes back to my ears: "Why do you tear at a wretched man, Aeneas? Spare the one who is now buried; spare your pious hands from defilement. Troy did not bring me forth a stranger to you, and this blood does not flow from the wood. Alas, flee these cruel lands, flee this greedy shore! For I am Polydorus. Here an iron crop of weapons covered me as I lay pierced through, and grew up over me in sharp javelins."
Thus, although wickedness may hide itself in a concealed cave, it is betrayed, so that it may pay the penalties it deserves.

sentences.en: The eternal law forbids violating the rights of another's bed and the marriage torches. The Julian law, which was laid down for Venus and for the mighty weapons of Cupid, deservedly yields to it.

You may look upon the daughter of Tyndareus, hiding in a secret place. She had hidden herself and sat, hated, at the altars, the common Fury of Troy and of her homeland, dreading the Teucrians, who were hostile to her because Pergamum had been overthrown, and the punishments of the Danaans, and the wrath of the husband she had deserted. Here let us be glad to remember that a just husband does not endure a wife joined to him in wedlock dissolving the laws they share, and yet being her own mistress and holding forth the marriage-torches as blameless.
Fires blazed up in my soul, and anger came over me to avenge my consort in her fall and to exact the penalty for the crime.
Shall she, forsooth, look unharmed upon these roofs and her familiar household gods? And will she go on, joined to the husband she has injured?

Not so. For although there is no memorable name to be won by punishing a woman, and the victory brings no praise, I shall still be praised for having extinguished this abomination and exacted the punishment she deserved. It will be a pleasure to have filled my soul with avenging flame, to have satisfied the ashes of that unspeakable crime, and to have kept this plague away from the marriage bed.
But the almighty Father does not by his command compel mortal hearts to preserve virginal modesty.

But you shall pay your vows to God and abide by your word. For faith must be kept with the Powers above, and the priest should tend the sacred rites chastely and lay his hands on the altars as a celibate.
Sweet thefts are mixed all too much with sad bitterness, for wealth gained by a thieving hand flows away of its own accord.

sentences.en: The sadder end of Cacus teaches this. Believing that he must live by plunder so that he might be rich and have plenty, he drove off from the stalls four bulls of outstanding build and as many heifers of surpassing beauty.

Meanwhile, when the son of Amphitryon was already moving his well-fed herds out of the stalls and preparing to leave, the cattle began to low at their departure, the whole grove was filled with their complaints, and the hills were left behind amid their clamour.
One of the cows returned the call and lowed beneath the vast cave, and, though closely guarded, she cheated Cacus of his hope.

For at this the grief of Alcides blazed up in fury with black gall. He seizes his arms in his hand, and his oak club heavy with knots, and at a run he makes for the steep heights of the airy mountain. Cacus, vomiting vain fires in the darkness, he seizes and clasps in a knot, and, clinging fast, he chokes him until his eyes are squeezed out and his throat is dry of blood.
At once the black house is laid open and its doors are torn away. The stolen cattle and the plunder he had forsworn are shown to the sky, and by the feet the shapeless corpse
is dragged out. Hearts cannot have their fill of gazing at the terrible eyes and face of the half-beast, his chest shaggy with bristles, and the fires extinguished in his jaws.
It is a great wickedness to harm a comrade's reputation, name, and honour, and to scatter ambiguous words among the crowd, for such words very often stir up harsh hatreds for many.
How many horrid wars did the elder Drances, hostile to the young Turnus, stir up with his tongue, his hatreds, and his accusation?

sentences.en: While mothers and wretched daughters-in-law, while the dear hearts of mourning sisters and boys bereft of their parents curse the harsh war and Turnus's marriage, and bid Turnus himself, who claims the kingdom of Italy and the highest honours for himself, decide the matter with arms, himself with the sword, fierce Drances aggravates all this and testifies that Turnus alone is being called, Turnus alone is demanded for the combat. He rises, burdens him with these words, and heaps up wrath.
You consult us, good King, on a matter that is obscure to no one and needs no voice of ours. Everyone admits that they know what the people's fortune brings, but they hesitate to speak.

Let him grant freedom of speech and relax his arrogance. Because of his unlucky auspices and sinister ways (I will say it, even though he threatens me with arms and death), we see that so many lights of our leaders have fallen and that the whole city has sunk in grief, while he attacks the Trojan camp, trusting in flight, and terrifies heaven with his arms.

He groans and bursts out with these words from the depths of his breast: You always have an ample flow of words, Drances, just when wars call for hands, and when the fathers are summoned, you are the first to arrive. But the senate-house is not to be filled with words, which fly from you abundantly and in safety as long as the rampart of the walls keeps the enemy at bay and the trenches are not overflowing with blood.
We are marching against the enemy. Why do you hold back? Or will your Mars always lie in your windy tongue and in those fleeing feet of yours? Will your right hand always be cold for war?

Am I defeated? Or will anyone, you foulest of men, justly claim that I am defeated, when he sees the swollen Tiber rising with Trojan blood, the whole house of Evander fallen together with its offspring, and the Arcadians stripped of their arms?
That is not how Bitias and huge Pandarus found me, nor the thousand men whom I, as victor, sent down to Tartarus in a single day.

sentences.en: A man who is consumed by a blind fire for another man's wife nourishes a wound in his veins. Even if he has never entered into these pacts, he is guilty of having broken the marriage bed.

But no diligence builds up their strength more than keeping away Venus and the goads of blind love. So they banish the bulls far away to lonely pastures, behind a mountain barrier and across glad rivers, or they keep them shut up indoors at full mangers. For the female gradually consumes their strength and burns them as they gaze at her, and she does not let them remember either the groves or the grass.

So that you steal nothing that belongs to another, draw in the sails of your desire entirely and blunt the wishes of your mind, holding on to nothing unjust, neither in burning desire nor in your heart. You shall not take the roofs of a house, or fields, or a yoke, or a lowly manservant or a lesser maidservant, or the hide of an ox, or the fleece of a slow ass: in short, nothing at all that the great world contains.

sentences.en: were rearing, together with their father Tyrrhus, whom the royal herds obey and to whom the custody of the plain far and wide is entrusted. The stag was accustomed to commands, and their sister Silvia, with every care, used to adorn its antlers, weaving soft garlands into them. She would comb the wild creature and wash it in a pure spring. Submitting to the hand and accustomed to its master's table, it used to wander in the woods, and then it would make its own way home again to the familiar threshold, however late at night.
As it wandered far off, the swift hounds of Iulus, out hunting, roused it, while by chance it was floating down the stream and relieving the heat on the green bank.
Ascanius himself, too, inflamed with the love of outstanding praise, aimed his arrows from his curved bow.

Nor did chance fail his erring right hand: the reed, driven with a loud whirr, went through the stag's belly and through its flanks. The wounded beast fled back within the familiar house and went moaning into its stall. Bleeding, like one imploring, it filled the whole house with its complaint.

Their sister Silvia was the first. Striking her arms with her palms, she calls for help and summons the hardy rustics. They arrive unlooked-for, since the fierce plague lurks in the silent woods: one armed with a fire-hardened brand, another with a heavy knotted club. Whatever each one found as he searched, anger makes into a weapon. Tyrrhus calls out the troops. As it happened, he had been splitting an oak into four with driven wedges, and now he snatches up his axe, breathing savagely.
Nor is the discord that spattered the Teucrians with so much Ausonian blood finished for you in grim war.

The fates wished you to lead your life under these auspices of theirs, and not to settle your cares by your own will. Therefore carry out the commands of God; let this be your greatest care. And just as ants, mindful of winter, plunder a huge heap of spelt and store it away in their home, the black column moves across the plains and carries its booty through the grass along a narrow path; some strain their shoulders to push the large grains of corn, others marshal the ranks and punish delays, and the whole path seethes with the work.

sentences.en: So the man whom the great glory of the highest things moves also undertakes labor himself for his own praise. Astonished by so great a warning and by the impulse of the Thunderer, he burns to depart in flight, to leave the sweet lands behind, and to expose his fearless head to a thousand dangers. There is one love in his heart: to seek the heavenly kingdoms. Let it be his delight to prepare arms and to bend to the strong oars. To this one love it is right for you to submit your spirit.

Let fierce fear drive them headlong to shake out the ropes in whatever direction and to spread the sails to unfavourable winds. Unless they hold their course between the two ways of death, Scylla and Charybdis, it is resolved to turn the sails back. Loose the sails swiftly! Look, a god sent from the high heavens urges us again to hasten our flight and to cut the twisted cables. I beg you, let no delay hold you back.

Like the Queen of the Sabaean peoples long ago, amazed at the words of the man who held the sceptre of the kingdom of the Solymi; or like the way she bore herself joyfully as she ruled over her own people, moving through their midst and urging on the work and her ancestral realm, when at the doors of Saba, in the middle of the temple's vault, surrounded by armed men and resting high upon her throne, she sat and gave rights and laws to men, and divided the labour of their tasks into fair shares, or perhaps lightened it: such is the bride of God. Surrounded by a crown of winged ones, enclosed by virgin choirs, bound with a tiara, and hiding her head among the clouds in sublime adornment, she gave five commandments to her flock and to her reborn offspring.

Not the founding of temples of solid marble to Phoebus and Trivia, and of a sacred day named after Phoebus, where the fire is in the middle and companions crown the bowl and call on Lenaeus as they pour libations; then Menalcas sets up contests of the swift javelin, with the target on an elm, and strips toughened bodies bare in the rustic wrestling-ground. This was the rite the farmers of old once kept.

sentences.en: But the nourishing mother Church commands that these days be kept with pious duties and that interrupted tasks be halted. She wishes the works and play of the exempted one to hang suspended, along with the huge threats of the walls and the ramparts raised level with the sky, and the hands of craftsmen to cease, their labour laid aside, so that her people may ponder heavenly gifts in their minds.

Yet on feast days it is lawful to do certain things that pious laws allow. No religious scruple has forbidden leading streams down, setting a hedge before the crop, laying snares for birds, burning brambles, or plunging the bleating flock into the healthful river. He has given the remaining days, in their order, as fortunate for work.

If the Aeneadae, named from a great name, once offered sacrifices to the Dionaean mother and to the gods as patrons of the works they had begun (if it is lawful to believe it), and were accustomed to sacrifice a varied bleating flock, and a shining bull to the High King of the heaven-dwellers; and if antiquity stands as a great witness in all lands that Alcides once won his own sacred rites by merit, when he seizes Cacus, who is vomiting vain fires in the darkness, clasps him in a knot, and, clinging to him, chokes him, his eyes squeezed out and his throat drained of blood:

if from that time the honor has been celebrated, and joyful descendants have observed the day, and Potitius, the first founder, and the Pinarian house, guardian of the Herculean rite, set up a great altar in the grove, what is the glory of the deed?
Who will relate how much better it is that the Thunderer's own sacred rites be duly celebrated and his altars loaded with gifts?
And to call upon the common God, by whose vengeance the dark house of Dis is immediately thrown open, its doors torn away?
And that the fathers, drawn forth, and the forsworn plunder are shown to heaven, while the dragon gnashes its teeth dreadfully?

sentences.en: Of praiseworthy Hippolytus, and Epidaurus, tamer of horses: those who press on with various pursuits as the time approaches, and devote all their care to swelling out with dense fat the one they have chosen as leader and named husband of the herd. They cut flowering grasses for him and supply him with streams and grain, so that he does not prove unequal to the pleasing labour and weak offspring do not reproduce the fasting of their fathers. But the herd itself they purposely thin down to leanness, and when the pleasure they now know provokes them to their first matings, they deny them leaves and keep them from the springs.
Often, too, they shake them with running and weary them in the sun, when the threshing floor groans heavily with the shorn crops and the empty chaff is tossed to the rising west wind.
They do this so that too much luxury may not leave its use too dulled for the generative field and clog the sluggish furrows.
In just the same way, intent in mind like a provident mother, the Bride of God wishes different people to be bound by different laws.
Those whom hard labour wears down, so that the grim gripes of a barking stomach may not break them, she relaxes her reins for, and in her piety she does not keep the weary flock from the mangers.

Boys and tender girls rejoice in the same lot, as do the woman in labor, the one who has just given birth, and the one nursing at the breast, feeble old men, the throng of beardless youth, and those who drag broken joints and exhausted limbs.

But those whose age is in the bloom of youthful years she knows how to restrain, just as she knows how to give loose reins to the wretched. (Although for wretched mortals each best day of life flees first, and fierce diseases come on, and labour and the harshness of hard death wear them down.) The feasts which by custom they are accustomed to tear with greedy teeth, the parent denies and forbids them, zealous for their salvation:

sentences.en: the roasted flesh of an ox or a boar, fat venison, and every kind of meat; nor is it lawful to feed on eggs for one with a barking stomach, who carries in his belly a rabid wolf, a grim thing for the stables, while there is a wondrous desire to chew, until hunger is taken away and the love of eating is suppressed. Let it please them to remember the Corycian, who had a few acres of abandoned land, land not fertile for bullocks, nor a crop suitable for flocks, nor fit for the vine; yet in spirit he matched the wealth of kings, and returning home late at night, he loaded his tables with unbought feasts.
For he had sparse greens among the brambles, and around them he planted white lilies, vervain, and the slender poppy; yet he kept away from himself any little greens greased with fat lard.

Imitate this old man, young people, you whose virtue is vigorous; let it stand firm in your mind never to break your mother's laws of fasting, and let it come to mind that it is beautiful to die in the pursuit of this virtue. In this way you will not despise common things.
A gentle bridle is the sorrow of a bruised heart, and the yearly confession of the stain you have committed, brought forth from the bottom of the heart into the ear of your own pastor.

You might refuse to reveal the fierce monsters of your crimes to your Cupentus, and so offer your breast exposed to the glowing iron, you who are terrified of savage fires; and shame might hinder your freedom to confess dreadful deeds. To prevent this, it has been granted to you by lot to present yourself at a trustworthy throne, and you choose the ear of those who take the place of the shepherds. For this right is granted to the guilty by established law.

Would that it pleased us to bind ourselves more often with this strap! That, however, is a matter of counsel. But we are bound by the command and warning of heaven to wash away our offenses once every year, once the year after our eleventh has come upon us.
If you fail to do this, may your mind be wounded by a heavier blow, and indeed be beyond the cure of any potent herbs.

sentences.en: The keeper who drives the slow little donkey never loads it with oil or cheap fruit, or brings back from the city on his return a hewn stone or a lump of black pitch, without sometimes unburdening the beast and easing its labor for several hours. For, as the poet testifies, what lacks alternating rest does not last.
What good does it do this man to be weighed down in vain by the mass of such great crimes through long cycles of rolling months?

Wretched one, you can unburden yourself if you wish, a sweet relief for your weariness; it is within your reach. All that remains is to confess your offenses. Then, if you please, I will lead you to the full mangers.
So that you do not find it burdensome to turn over the bristling field and break up its clods, I will scatter the hiding places and recesses of the soul.

The horses of the Sun bring back the sacred feast of Easter in their four-horse chariot. The very Son of God presents himself at the holy altars. Standing there, he invites the people and proclaims honor for the temples, and he wishes his own to see to the banquets, rejoicing together, while above all he gladdens the new dishes with abundant wine, pouring heavenly wines from bowls as a new nectar, the gifts and the joy of God. And all of this is free, for with him a price counts for nothing: he gives every single thing unbought.

sentences.en: Look: the inner house is being furnished, splendid with royal luxury, and banquets lie open in the middle of the temples. There are garments worked with skill and proud purple, massive silver on the altars, and, chased in gold, the brave deeds of the fathers, a very long series of events.
Many gather, bidden to recline on couches painted with varied flowers, with fragrant garlands on every side.
Servants give water for the hands, serve bread from baskets and bring napkins with shorn nap.

Just as the life of men on earth is renewed and nourished by a sevenfold kind of things, so that which has been seen as the one salvation of the soul for mortals rightly demands for itself seven mystical gifts from the sacred shrines, which heal wounded hearts. Let antiquity stand as a great witness to the faith.

Let the Shepherd not refuse to apply healing hands to the wounds, nor burden God by demanding better omens. For the fates preserve this man: he feeds on the ethereal air and never lies dead among the cruel shades, even though his mind is covered with vices and very close to death, if only, groaning much, he diligently washes himself with that draught and takes these cups of medicine for the soul.

It will not be the way of death, however much a fiery thirst, driven through all the veins, has burned up his wretched limbs. He will not die like a calf in the lush grass, nor yield up his sweet soul at the full mangers. On the contrary, these very things are destruction to the wolves. Restored by furies, they will burn, and they themselves, now under a sick death (may fate grant better things to the pious, and that burning to the enemies), will tear their own torn limbs with bare teeth.

sentences.en: Neither the shade of lofty groves nor heavenly meadows can move the mind, nor the stream, purer than amber, that rolls over the rocks and seeks the plain. Instead the lowest flanks give way, a stupor weighs upon the sluggish eyes, and the neck droops to the earth with its downward weight.
Here the sevenfold order of nature's aid is unrolled. First of all, at the rising of the light we are brought forth into the breezes.

But scarcely has this fleshly mass, drawn out by a sorrowful birth, come forth into the light when at once it desires that the beginning of its body be strengthened on every side with gathered strength, and that it grow and increase until it puts on firm bones and muscles and exercises the great joints of its limbs.

So that the body may then stand firm on its own sinews, hunger must be taken away with feasts, and at the same time the mouth must be moistened with a bowl of foaming Bacchus, unless perhaps in the heat it is better for the thirsty mouth to quench its thirst with a leaping stream of sweet water, or custom so requires.

And since a pitiable storm of the sky frequently arises through disease, laying waste to everything far and wide around, and no whirlwind driving a storm rushes over the sea as thickly as the many plagues of cattle, which also suddenly seize the bodies of men and a whole race from its origin, Iapis is therefore sought, beloved by Phoebus above all others, who, an old man girt in his cloak in the manner of a physician,
Nor is it enough for physicians to shut out the causes of diseases unless, driving away the remnants, you restore with aids the strength broken by the whirlwind of disease and strengthen its vigor.
