sentences.en: The more their strength is exhausted, the more fiercely they all press on to repair the ruins of the fallen race.
Now a twofold restoration of our race remains: one part proclaims the laws of the forum and human justice, and the other opens the homes of Astraea and of Heaven.
Nurturing mother of Christians, resting on the pillars of faith, since you are joined in a stable marriage and dedicated to Christ, come, bearing children, supply offspring for both these courts.

Make it your care to add special honors to the leaders themselves, and to foster the life of the skilled who preside over the rest: both those who handle civil affairs, pondering the laws (and so wear the civic oak shading their temples), and those who handle heavenly things and, by the command of the eternal Deity, fill the benches by their office.

First of all, the soul has its own beginnings of life. Bathed in the purifying water of the salt sprinkling, we draw the vital air as if newly born. The mind, weighed down by the heavier burden of Adam's stain and buried before in death, is called back from gloomy Orcus and, cleansed by the rays of justice, is reborn innocent.

For as soon as the power of the heavenly water, descending sacredly to the breast, touches the body, the old shadow perishes and a new light arises. It is like a smoky cloud that is sometimes lifted high into the upper air: first it kindles with the flashes of the sun; then, driving away the smoke, it is clothed in light and gleams far and wide; finally, with its radiant flames, it becomes a rival of the Sun.

sentences.en: Then the fiery vigour of the divine breath within strengthens the powers with might and supplies the courage by which you may conquer or fall in a brave death.

There is no need for Achates to strike a spark from flint, catch the fire in leaves, heap dry fuel around it and snatch the flame into the tinder. At once the devouring fire is rolled by the wind to the highest rooftops, the flames surge over, and the heat rages up to the breezes of a breast intent, in its zeal, on catching the breaths of heavenly life. Just so, once, the companions strained, Christ's band of twelve, their breasts kindled with cares like children bereft of a lost parent. For twice five days they kept silent, stayed behind the closed door, prayed with one mind and demanded the promises of the Lord.

Then suddenly the heavens thundered, and the high roofs seemed to be shaken mightily, as once by the whirlwind of an oncoming wind, and the house seemed to be filled with terror. While they were afraid, the huge sky thundered more and more with manifold flame; then a tongue with flashing rays, coming thick and fast like snow, scattered sparks of fire.

At once they were astounded in their minds and humbly acknowledge the promised gifts. They do not so much greet the signs sent down from the sky with an eager shout as double their fervent prayers in silent fear. No less does the upper air roar, and flaming fleeces glide down from the high sky. The sounds were heard all the more because of this, while, with much lightning and in divided order, a flashing tongue of fire, harmless and soft to the touch, sat on the head of each of them. A crest burns on each head. Then the Holy Spirit fills their breasts and, breathing gently, embraces their senses with an ethereal breeze and entwines fire in their minds.
This is the way we must enter upon, this the sea we must plow, so that we may rejoice in the favoring breath of the breeze.

lines.en: of changed bread into the limbs of the divine body,

sentences.en: It is certain that by the soul's food strength grows for the living, and that the powers within are increased for brave deeds. But what nourishment fills men with bold spirits?
Nothing better than these can be given to the human race from the fruits of the high Deity, as a gift of the gods.

O Father, O boundless mercy, God most good, with what food do you restore souls? How sumptuous are the wines you are pleased to have given to our palate, with which we may celebrate the sober mysteries of sacred Bacchus in the manner of our ancestors!

For your Bride lives on and thrives, your pledges, O Christ, having embraced your body, having embraced your blood, having embraced the feasts and cups of the divine table, your gifts, O Christ, and the monuments of your cruel pain.

But indeed, when we place our gifts on the incense-burning altars, we believe that the meager bread is changed into the limbs of an immense body; and this too, wonderful to say (forbear to shake faith), that the sacred liquids shine and the wines we see turn themselves into rosy blood.

O Son of the highest Father, my great power, my strength, what flames does the ample virtue of your supper and of the rosy blood entwine in the mind, what fires in the bones, among the heavenly tables and the Bacchic liquid?
And that immense courage is drawn in, while the hostile force rages with bloody slaughter, while the innocent is destroyed by the sword?

Come, tell me, what is the appearance of things? How great a change has brought them back for the better? What correction of morals is there where these sacred rites thrive and this fruitful chalice is used more often? O you whose blood courses untouched by age and whose strength is solid in its own vigor, do not be reluctant to say whom these divine liquids have not made eloquent, kindled with a great love of piety. Alas, why do we still allow the delights of the Lord, known above the ether, to be foul to our palate!

lines.en: And at the same time you will be satisfied with the rich delights of the Lord,

sentences.en: O wretched minds of men, O blind hearts, whom impiety and forgetfulness of ancestral faith have compelled to violate, with the hand and with bold jaws, the disc of bread changed into the limbs of the divine body, and to use rustic fruits instead of sacred banquets!
Woe likewise to those whom lack of food has driven, with unclean hearts, to turn their bites against this kind of fruit.
Woe also to the faithless faithful, whom, driven by laws, it is right to compel by force to recline at the tables of the gods.
I would have these people remember that they are true Latins, the race of Christians, righteous not by bond or by laws, but holding itself of its own accord to the custom of the eternal God.

When the Trojans had eaten up their feast, and extreme want compelled them to turn their bites against the scanty Ceres and not to spare the fateful crust, the broad squares, Iulus said, "Hey, we are even eating our tables!" He joked no further. Once heard, that voice first brought an end to their labors, and his father caught it up as it first fell from the speaker's mouth and, astounded by the divine will, held it fast. At once he said: "Hail, land owed to me by the fates, and you, O faithful household gods of Troy, hail! Here is our home, this is our country. For my father Anchises, I now recall, left me these secrets of the fates:
'When, son, you have been carried to unknown shores and hunger, your food cut short, compels you to eat your tables,
then, weary as you are, remember to hope for homes, and there to set your first dwellings with your own hand and build them behind a rampart.'"

You are deceived, Aeneas, greatly deceived, guest. That was not the final hunger awaiting you, the one that would put an end to your ruin. Rather, as the holy monuments of God teach, it is the spelt cakes, now known in the sacred rites of Christians, and the abundant streams of the Lamb's poured-out blood that will bring an end to labors. So, O race brought forth under better fates, let it be an immense shame and a great impiety for you to be driven to the dishes of so great a table by the compelling command and authority of the great parent of the gods. Let there be no need to use force on you; rather, may you come of your own accord.

sentences.en: Let your seasonings, to stir a sluggish taste, be piety, hoary faith, and the fervor of love. For the flavor will plainly prove itself and will soothe the mouths of those who try its sweetness with a friendly sensation. At the same time you will be satisfied with the Lord's rich delights, you will begin to be moved alike by the pure wine and by the gifts, and you will fulfil the great love of the true Father.
Shall hearts, then, O Christ, languish under grievous disease, and will you not pity bruised souls and shattered fortunes?

If Venus, shaken by her son's undeserved pain, plucked as a mother dittany from Cretan Ida, a stalk with downy leaves, crowned with a purple flower (a herb not unknown to wild goats when winged arrows have lodged in their backs); if Venus, her face veiled in a dense cloud, brought this down, and with it tinctured the dark water in the gleaming basins, secretly medicating it, and sprinkled in the healthful juices of ambrosia and fragrant panacea:

With that water the aged Iapis, unknowing, bathed the wound, and suddenly all the pain fled from the body, all the blood was stanched deep in the wound, and now the arrow, following his hand, fell out with no one forcing it, and fresh strength returned for the battle.

sentences.en: What he willed at the same time in curing the sore wounds of his children's minds: let not Apollo presume to be held the founder of this medical art; nature gave potent herbs no way to it; but Jesus alone cures every kind of disease and the deeply gaping wounds of his beloved offspring. Meanwhile he willed that the guilty should confess every crime, then beat their breasts with their palms and heave a mighty groan from the depth of the heart, and so at last be loosed from their bonds by the ministering key, which God instituted for the sake of removing the death of the mind laid low by the lethal blow of a wound.
He instituted it when the acorns and arbutus berries of the sacred woods were already failing and Dodona was denying sustenance.

Yet unless you pursue the earth with constant harrows, prune back the shadows with a sickle, and call upon the rain with vows, alas, you will wait in vain for another's great heap, and you will console your hunger in the woods by shaking an oak. Thus labor is added to the earth of the mind, so that baneful blight might eat the stalks and the lazy thistle might bristle in the fields: the crops perish, a rough wood springs up, burrs and caltrops, and among the shining cultivated lands the unlucky darnel and barren wild oats hold sway.

Hence the mind has its own weapons, just as rustic gifts do: the plowshare, and first the heavy oak of the curved plow, the slow-rolling wagons of the Eleusinian mother, threshing-sledges, drags and harrows of oppressive weight, and besides these the wicker-work of Celeus, cheap equipment, arbutus hurdles, and the mystic winnowing-fan of Iacchus. These three parts supply you with weapons once you have confessed, especially when many predictions of former prophets terrify with dreadful warning: a cry strikes the upper air.

You are beaten, and you feel cares deeply in your tamed breast, just as the mourning nightingale under the poplar shade laments her lost young, which a harsh plowman spotted and dragged unfledged from the nest; but she weeps through the night, and sitting on a branch renews her pitiful song and fills the places far and wide with mournful complaints, dripping with a shower. Truly, tears do not roll down in vain: the mind remains unmoved in good, and it is settled in the heart to have atoned for its offenses, until the dregs are conquered by grief.

marginalia.text: Per tribulas, trahas, rastra dentibus armata, quibus terra pungitur & conteritur, insinuandam duxi cordis nostri compunctionem, vt est prima pars pœnitentiæ. Per aratrum verò, & vomerem, quo terra aperitur, euertitur, & quasi euomitur, confessionem ipsam, quæ est secunda pars eiusdem Sacramenti, non incongruè intelligendam putaui, quatenus ipsa confessione nostram conscientiam Christi vicario aperimus, & sordes animi eruimus. Per mysticam denique vannum, qua purgatur frumentum, & à palea secernitur, vti etiam per tarda Eleusinæ matris voluentia plaustra, quibus seges in horreum inuehitur, satisfactionem intelligo, qua mouemur ad faciendos fructus dignos pœnitentiæ. Luc. 3.
marginalia.text_en: By the threshing-sledges, drags, and harrows armed with teeth, by which the earth is pricked and crushed, I considered that the compunction of our heart should be suggested, as it is the first part of penance. But by the plough, and the ploughshare, by which the earth is opened, turned over, and as it were vomited out, I thought that confession itself, which is the second part of the same Sacrament, should not incongruously be understood, insofar as by confession itself we open our conscience to the vicar of Christ, and root out the filth of the soul. Finally, by the mystic winnowing fan, by which the grain is purged and separated from the chaff, as also by the slow-rolling wagons of the Eleusinian mother, by which the crop is carried into the barn, I understand satisfaction, by which we are moved to produce fruits worthy of penance. Luke 3.
marginalia.explanation: The entire farming sequence is an explicit three-part allegory of the sacrament of penance: harrowing is contrition, ploughing is confession, and winnowing and carting the crop are satisfaction.

marginalia.text_en: Satisfaction.

sentences.en: …of greater crimes, which one is then not ashamed to confess, so that a most holy life may follow, late though it may be; so that, once the sins committed have been sent down into dark Tartarus, Astraea may return bright from heaven and revisit the earth, bringing back the ancient examples of the saints' virtue.

But the compassion of Christ, wishing to soothe the grieving soul with consolation and to turn away its cares with prayers, groaning deeply and shaken in mind by great grief, added to these another help for the mind, for the time when the Fate draws out the last threads of life and the hostile force draws near. It ordained that a priest in a pure vestment should come forth and, bearing bowls of sacred oil, should touch the sick man, with prayers poured out to the stars, so that he may take away the remnants of sin, and so that life, health and new strength may return to the languishing man as before.
But now the ruin of the fallen race that must be repaired is twofold, and for these a double medicine has been granted for their salvation.

sentences.en: Hence, so that no one may contemplate a secret love, call it marriage and cloak his fault with that name, and so that this evil may not creep more widely, the divine powers have granted that the social pacts of the bed be confirmed by law in stable wedlock with a solemn rite. Let it be pleasing to lead solemn processions to the shrines.

And since the bonds of marriage are the concern of God alone, with Juno excluded, and Phoebus, and the Lyaeus of Erebus, and law-giving Ceres, as they call her, and the migrating shades, we burn due honors to Christ alone at the altars of the Deity, renewing the day with gifts.

Special honors are deservedly appointed to holy Orders, for on these rests the leaning house, the mystical house of the Christians. To these it is given by lot to repair the ruins of the fallen race of priests and the temples stripped of ministers, and to them is given the full power to restore them. They create the whole race of sacrificers who may appease the divine powers.
Standing, these heap the altars with heavenly bowls, and in the holy sanctuaries they make ready the chalice of the bloody liquid, the implements of Ceres, and the consecrated fruits.
What of the fact that Holy Order also supplies us with strength for brave deeds, moving our inner being with the favorable breath of the Zephyr of the eternal Deity, which it bestows as its gift?
If Orders were done away with, who would be able to render the Father his due rights and offer sacred gifts to God at the smoking altars?

sentences.en: Hence the altars do not burn with the entrails laid on them, and the Prophet, when consulted, cannot give answers. In vain does empty superstition, as a suppliant, lay its tribute on the altars: it is too hostile to the Thunderer.

So whoever presents himself as a Priest through a counterfeit Order, intending to deceive by offering feigned sacrifices to the Heavenly ones, will not get away with it unpunished. For such daring deeds he will find that he has paid for his offenses with no ordinary penalty, and he will make it known to all that the guilty man has paid for his crime.

Be warned: learn Justice, and learn not to slight the Deity. By this twofold duty let us be borne on high. If retracing our steps this way and escaping to the upper air is hard work, the descent to Avernus, on the other hand, is easy. Hyblaean honey is mixed with the difficult, but bitterness with the easy, and in place of a heavy, grim yoke you bring back one that is light and sweet.
Greatest Leader of the Christians, as long as you are safe, I will never admit that the affairs of our soul or our kingdoms are defeated.

For help in war, our strength is meager in proportion to the divine power of the gods. On one side we are surrounded by arms; on the other, madness torments us; and within are a thousand fears. But I am preparing to join to you mighty peoples and camps rich in kingdoms, a salvation that unexpected fortune holds out: you bring yourself here at the demand of the fates.
If you allow yourself to be added as a guide to these thousands, the matter is safe; with you as our guide, we shall rule the stars of heaven.

sentences.en: A race hostile to you is sailing the Lethean sea. Since you have the power, see to it that it does not land on our shores: strike force into the winds, and sink and overwhelm their ships.

There are said to be twin plagues, called the Dirae, whom the dead of Night bore in one and the same birth together with Tartarean Megaera. She bound them with equal coils of serpents and gave them windy wings.
From this I conclude that human stain is of two kinds. One is the kind drawn from our first origin.
when they consumed the forbidden food. But their unknowing descendants, liable for another's fault, drank in the grim poison, and the sons reproduce the contagion of their fathers.

From this came that first stain of evil. From this the wicked plague settled in the veins and flowed abundantly with gore, infecting mankind. From this the joyless wound was inflicted on the soul, a wound that no power and no human art could heal. Instead the deadly touch grows from its tinder: the furious evil of the serpent descends through the whole body, insinuates its hidden powers into the silent senses, and grows as it goes.

sentences.en: She also has another offspring, a heap of venial fault. Although it does not make the Deity unfriendly to us, minds defiled by these stains are soon disciplined with punishments after death and pay the penalties for their old wrongs. For some, the crime they have taken on is washed away beneath a vast whirlpool; for others, it is burned out by fire.

O faith of gods and men! A second Mezentius, supreme despiser of the gods, more cruel than he who once used to join dead bodies to the living, fitting hands to hands and mouths to mouths (a kind of torture), and so killed them with a lingering death as they dripped with gore and putrefaction in that wretched embrace.

Harsher than this, I say, the madness of sin pours itself forth with loosened reins, throwing everything around into confusion far and wide, while by a deadly crime it joins wretched minds, deprived of vital light, to living bodies.

When the weary citizens want to surround this enemy as he rages with unspeakable deeds, he slips away into the fields of his allies, takes refuge there, and is defended by the arms of his threefold host. For the one who suggests shameful things arms this enemy's side, when he infects the breezes of the human breast with Stygian blasts, spreading poisons from his foul mouth.
Vicious Pleasure joins herself to him as an ally in crimes, leading out feminine troops with crescent shields; for whom, like a consuming fire and a soft flame, the marrow

we must take skilful care lest she devour the inner parts of the mind. For Cytherea is turning over new arts and new counsels in her breast, so that Cupid, changed in face and features, may come in place of sweet Christ, inflame raging minds with gifts, and entwine fire in their bones.
Third from the camp comes the worst beast of all, who by her nod, beyond the rest, strengthens the scepters of so dire a Tyrant. For to what does dire assent not drive mortal hearts?

sentences.en: Therefore let all boldness, rising with just fury, demand the King for punishment in immediate battle, and make ready to carry the standards. O chosen youth of the gods above, flower of the ancients and valor of men, whom just grief carries against the enemy and whom the impious King inflames with deserved anger: to arms, men, take arms in hand, and let reason supply the arms! For we see the enemy battle lines standing on this height, and here a sudden cloud gathering with black dust. We comrades look out and see darkness rising over the plains. Caicus is the first to shout from the opposite mound: "What mass is this, citizens, rolling along in black gloom?"

Bring the sword quickly, hand out weapons, and climb the walls: the enemy is here! To draw up a battle line and trust ourselves to the plain is not advisable now; we see what our fortune is. Let us therefore guard the camp and the walls made safe by the rampart.
Tell me, Calchas: how many leaders of this host have issued from the gates of the rampart, and what kind of leaders are they, and how great?

Twice I have approached this camp of crimes as a scout. I have surveyed its battle lines, and I will reveal the secrets I know. It is right to hate these men and to bring into the open air everything they hide, so that I may not be bound by any laws of crime.
The foremost leader of the war, who wields the reins, boasts of himself under the unjust title and name of Lucifer. For he is a horrendous, huge monster whose light has been taken away.
Unable in his mind to bear that he is shut out of the empyrean kingdom, the fated fields, and that his scepter is transferred to a mortal settler, he stirs up the fires of the Furies.

It was not enough for him to have sharpened his first furies against heaven and to have wished, in vain, to overturn the council and the whole house of the Thunderer. Now he longs to involve this race of ours in the punishments of Erebus. To this end he brings all his zeal and all his efforts; against us he directs his thunderbolts of war, though in vain, as we hope, while the fates resist him.

sentences.en: Yet the audacious one, though defeated, does not lose confidence. Of his own accord he rouses their spirits with his words, and of his own accord he rebukes the sevenfold battle lines that he leads out onto the open plain. Then, raging in his mind and tossed on the tide of his anger, gnashing his teeth, he thunders these words from his savage mouth: "Shall kindly fates help the Christ-worshippers? God's mind has turned against them and snatched away the help they were used to. They will not escape our weapons or our fires. The seas are impassable to Christ himself, and there is no hope of flight; the other half of the world has been taken from them.

But the land is in our hands, and so many thousands of the heretical race bear arms. Fated things do not terrify me at all. If they boast of any oracles of the Thunderer on their own behalf, enough has been granted to the fates and to Mary in having restored so many thousands of the fallen to the kingdom of heaven. I too have fates of my own that oppose theirs: to cut down the accursed Catholic race with the sword without delay. Let them not fear darkness, or cowardly thefts of the Palladium with the guards of the topmost citadel slain; we shall not hide in the blind belly of a horse. It is resolved to surround their walls with fire openly, in broad daylight. I shall see to it that they say they are dealing with no Danaans or Pelasgian youth, whom Hector held off into the tenth year."

Their spirits roused by these words, the cohorts dare to advance, to join battle, and to charge farther forward. Once more the seven chief leaders descend into the fray and send their lives into open danger. A shout goes up along all the walls and across the ramparts; they bend their keen bows and whirl their throwing-thongs. The whole ground is strewn with missiles; then shields and hollow helmets ring from the blows, and a fierce battle rises. It is like the great rainstorm that comes from the west under the rainy Kids and lashes the ground, or as thick as the hail with which storm-clouds plunge into the shallows, when Jupiter, bristling with south winds, whirls a watery tempest and bursts the hollow clouds in the sky.

When matters were at last settled and the tumult had ceased, Calchas went on with his discourse and of his own accord added this: "Has any word perhaps reached your ears about these seven Leaders, the sinews and strength of the opposing side? Know for certain that they exist, and with renowned fame besides.
Have they perhaps earned any name and honour by their counsels, or outstanding praise by brave deeds?

sentences.en: Or they can proclaim their forefathers and the ancient names of their grandsires, and a whole lineage traced through Latin kings.

Begotten of Vice as their father, they betray themselves by the work of their crimes. For it belongs to the first to attempt a way by which he can raise himself and what is his from the ground, flit victorious on the lips of men, prance upon the ground, and gather up his proud steps.

Thus straightway, before your eyes, Dares lifts his face with vast strength and raises himself amid a great murmur of men. He alone was wont to contend against Paris. At the tomb where greatest Hector lies, he struck down the victorious Butes, a man of immense body who boasted that he came from the Bebrycian race of Amycus, and stretched him dying on the tawny sand. Thus, I say, Dares extols himself with praises from a swollen mouth. He displays his broad shoulders, stretches out and tosses his arms by turns, and lashes the air with blows, so that he betrays the arrogance of his breast and his haughty mind.

But to this one Avarice gives ill-counselling hunger and the dread lust of having. Let him be called by the infamous name of Pygmalion, more monstrous in crime than all others, who secretly slew the unwary Sychaeus with a cruel sword. Or let him be called the equal of the Thracian who, seized by a like love and breaking all divine law, butchers Polydorus and takes the gold by force. To what do you not drive mortal breasts, accursed hunger for gold, most harsh in the pursuit of gain?
The foul plague of Venus bestows an ignoble lineage on another, who invaded his daughter's chamber and a forbidden marriage, and whose limbs roving lust shamefully devours.

Unhappy Dido burns with this and wanders raging through the whole city, like a hind struck by an arrow. From afar, amid the Cretan woods, a shepherd hunting with darts has pierced her while she was off her guard, and unknowingly left the flying steel in her. In flight she ranges the forests and glades of Dicte, and the deadly shaft clings to her side.
But Envy, the fourth monster, torments herself with the swollen ulcer of an inflated crime, so that her flanks may burst.
Drances once felt this, for the glory of Turnus drove him on with sidelong envy and bitter goads.

sentences.en: By what furies is he driven? Look: sparks fly off from the whole face of the blazing man, and fire flashes from his fierce eyes. It is just as when a bull, before his first battles, raises terrifying bellows and tries to throw his wrath into his horns, pushing against the trunk of a tree; he assails the winds with blows and rehearses for the fight by scattering the sand.
Or it is as with Alcides, when frenzy and wrath drive his mind headlong, and he gnashes his teeth and thunders dreadfully with his arms.
He is as huge as Athos, or as huge as Eryx, or as huge as father Apennine himself when he roars with his quivering holm-oaks and rejoices to lift himself with his snowy peak to the breezes.

The sixth, the devourer of things, is filled with old wine and rich venison as a swift whirlpool swallows things in the sea. Taking up bowls of unmixed wine, he drains the foaming cup with no sluggishness and drenches himself from the brimming gold. And just as Circe, the cruel goddess, once did with her potent herbs, he changes us from the appearance of men into the features and faces of wild beasts.
Hence groans are heard, and the rage of lions refusing their chains and roaring late in the night; bristly swine and bears are heard raging in their pens, and the shapes of great wolves howling.

He is such, and as huge, as Polyphemus was in his hollow cave. As soon as Polyphemus was glutted with the feast and buried in wine, he laid down his drooping neck and lay sprawled through the immense cave, belching gore and gobbets mixed with bloody wine in his sleep. Soon he is surrounded on every side, and his huge eye is bored through with a sharp weapon. It was his only eye, and it lay hidden beneath his grim brow, like an Argive shield or the lamp of Phoebus.

Finally, the last is judged to have earned, by his own hand, a place among the cattle because of his sluggishness; nothing more is granted him. So Sloth gives him a name that fits his deserts. For the kindly light never rouses this idler, nor do the morning songs of the birds beneath the roof, accustomed as he now is to snoring until Aurora, with her rosy four-horse chariot, has crossed the middle of the sky on her heavenly course.

sentences.en: Under his leadership, in the furrows where we have often sown barley, wretched darnel and barren wild oats hold sway; and instead of the soft violet and the purple narcissus, up spring the thistle and the Christ's-thorn with its sharp spines.

Relying on this omen, the son of Hyrtacus at once attacks with his sword the proud Rhamnes, who happened to be propped up on high carpets, breathing out sleep from his whole chest. He was himself a king, and an augur most dear to King Turnus, but he could not ward off destruction by his augury.

Nearby he crushes three attendants lying at random among the weapons, and the armour-bearer of Remus. He finds the charioteer beneath the very horses and with his sword severs their drooping necks. Then he takes the head from the master himself and leaves the trunk heaving with black blood. Warmed by the gore, the earth and the couches are drenched. So too Lamyrus and Lamus, and young Serranus, handsome of face, who had played long into that night and lay with his limbs overcome by much wine. Happy he would have been had he kept that game going the whole night through and carried it on into daylight.

We have a supreme leader, most renowned in arms and mighty in war; alone he would stand against a thousand ranks, and this heavenly armour-bearer would overcome a thousand Camillas. The crest on his head blazes, flame pours from his plumes and the top of his helmet, and his golden shield-boss spews out vast fires, just as when, on a clear night, blood-red comets glow ominously, or the blaze of Sirius, which rises bringing thirst and disease to sick mortals and saddens the sky with its baleful light.

At the sight of him the bravest Hector is a boy; a boy too is Aegaeon, who, they say, had a hundred arms and a hundred hands, and fire blazed from his fifty mouths and chests when, against the thunderbolts of Jove, he clashed as many matching shields and drew as many swords.
The battle-lines of the winged ones have joined us, so many thunderbolts of war; and finally a thousand phalanxes come to our aid: the might of the Christ-born, the flower of men, the chosen youth.
Meanwhile, even with forces so great, no one is to win victory with an idle hand, but only by brave deeds.

sentences.en: There a grim battle is joined under an ill-starred omen, where strength is great and fear has lent wings to the feet. So when a people is bereft of fear, the watch whiles away the sleepless night in play, and young men with crimson crests, gleaming with gold, sprawl across the grass, indulge in wine and tip up the bronze mixing-bowls.
Even one mighty in war, if he despises the enemy too greatly, will fall before evening returns with Olympus closed.

Hence the sentinels on watch must drive dangers away from the citadel, and also, trembling with dread, inspect the gates, join the bridges and ramparts, and bear arms. Let keen Fear and Love of the Thunderer press on: these the almighty Father appointed, should adversity ever call, to be rulers of the young and masters of affairs.
Let every legion along the walls, having drawn its share of danger by lot, keep watch, and then take turns at whatever each must guard.

But if the mind has long been stirring to join battle or to undertake some great deed, and is not content with calm repose, and if anyone has a spirit that scorns the light and believes that the honour it strives for is well bought with life, then the squadrons of the seven virtues, turned against them, to clash
with the opposing Captains of the vices. O would that, roused, it made them eager, for they would rush ready into war.

The virtue whose name is Submission heard this and, in her zeal to seek the lofty heights above, of her own accord offers her willing obedience, though she herself is heavily smitten by fear of praise. The bountiful giver of goods, whose care is gifts, was burning to join herself as an ally in the highest affairs.
God adds this ardour to the minds of the rest, who dig their spurs into the shoulders of their foaming horses, and the hoof shakes the crumbling plain with four-footed thunder.

Chaste devotee of purity and of snow-white modesty, resplendent in slender fare and moderate dress, the Rule of Virtue advances and follows her sister; with equal steps the gentle heroine hastens hither,

sentences.en: But diligent Piety joins these as their comrade in arms. She leads a column of horsemen and troops gleaming with bronze. She is a warrior whose woman's hand is not used to the distaff or to Minerva's wool-baskets; she is a virgin used to enduring hard battles and to outstripping the winds with her swift feet. She could fly over the topmost blades of an untouched crop of grass and not harm the tender ears of grain as she ran. Or she could make her way through the midst of the sea, held up above the swelling wave, without wetting her swift soles in the water.
They share one love, to destroy the plagues of vice; yet first they kindle the altars with chaste gifts.
Come then, put aside your fear and hope for certain salvation, while Piety, while hoary Faith, and hearts invincible in war fight it out, ready to conquer the rebels.
These, set against the gentle Zephyr of the divine Godhead's breeze, reveal themselves under various names as six monsters of crime.

This one slackens the reins of God's mercy too far and tightens those of his justice more than is just, pulling back the bridle, since it was begotten by our race's self-confidence. Hence it is rightly given the name Presumption.

sentences.en: It is right for anyone to trust in the Gods against their will. Often the human mind, steeped in this sweet poison, reasons with itself in this way, counterfeiting the color of truth: if it is our lot to live like an upturned tree, then nature has various ways of producing various trees. For some come up of themselves, of their own accord, with no one forcing them, and spread far and wide over the plains and the winding rivers, like the soft osier and the pliant broom, the poplar, and the willow groves whitening with grey-green leaves.

Others need no root, and the pruner does not hesitate to return the topmost shoot to the earth and entrust it there. Indeed, even when the trunks are cut, wonderful to tell, an olive root pushes out from the dry wood. And so we see the branches of one tree turn harmlessly into those of another: the pear-tree, changed, bears grafted apples, and stony cornels redden on plum-trees. But I, a wild olive grafted onto the trunk of a long-lived olive, could I not hope for wholesome offspring?
Should none of the woods expect the pressed-down arches of layered shoots, or living nurseries in their own soil?

Those that raise themselves of their own accord into the breezes of the light rise unfruitful, it is true, but lush and strong, for natural vigor is in the soil. Yet if anyone grafts these too, or transplants them and entrusts them to well-worked trenches, they will shed their wild spirit, and with no labor they will quickly follow into whatever arts you wish.
And the barren shoot that comes up from the lowest roots will also do this, if it is set out through open fields.
What need is there, then, of many things and of frequent cultivation? Go far away, cares; let me pursue leisure like good Daphnis.

Opposed to this is a plague that is given the name Diffidence. She rages savagely with monstrous deeds, rolling her bloodshot gaze, her trembling cheeks flecked with spots, and she is pale with the death to be endured.
Almighty God does not drive as many with his thunderbolt to the shades, the pale ghosts of Erebus, and the deep night, as this one has caused to break off their burdensome life as soon as possible,

marginalia.text_en: For formally, heretics have reached such a pitch of obstinacy that, when they are refuted by the force of arguments, they refuse to be convinced that they are wrong: hence they turn to evasions.

sentences.en: urging them on to slaughter: this one to impale himself on a bloody blade and drive the cruel sword through his ribs; that one to throw himself headlong from high towers, to rush onto cliffs or rocks, or to drown himself in the waves, or to find a way to free himself from these cares by some other kind of death. Deceit or valor: who would ask which, in an enemy?
He sings this to ears that are not deaf: that for the accursed man there will be one safety for the conquered, to hope for no safety.
But dread Celaeno, leading a third troop, joins herself to these, together with the other Harpies, whom horrid Orcus vomits forth.

No monster is grimmer than they, and no fiercer plague or wrath of God has ever risen from the Stygian waves. These birds have the faces of maidens, the foulest discharge from their bellies, hooked hands, and faces always pale with hunger. But they have indeed left their former tables. So when we feast on delicacies and rich banquets, the Harpies suddenly appear, swooping down from the mountains with a horrifying rush; they beat their wings with a loud clangor, plunder the feast, and befoul everything with their filthy touch. Then comes a dread cry amid the foul stench: whom might this breed of foul monster, and this foulest discharge of the belly, signify? Whom am I to believe is marked by this filth?
Those infected with the plague of heresy, whose hearts delight in impious pursuits, forever like a Fury common to their country.

These have willingly left the sumptuous tables of truth, so that they might spread false meanings under the image of truth. So, while they fill their black gullets with foul filth, bitter hunger presses them, and their appetite for eating is not appeased. And so, when we are refreshed with the delights of truth at the altars, a noisy throng soon comes from the opposite quarter of heaven and from hidden lairs, flies around the prey with hooked feet, and defiles the feast with its mouth, mingling sacred things with profane; its zeal is to confound the known words of truth.

O if only the comrades would attack and attempt new battles, maiming with the sword the obscene birds of the sea! But they take no force on their feathers and no wounds on their backs; gliding off in swift flight beneath the stars, they leave behind the half-eaten prey and foul traces.

sentences.en: There will never be a lack of hostile men, whom their brothers' glory will drive with the bitter goads of sidelong Envy, when heavenly matters go well for those brothers and thence honour, a great name, and glory accrue to Christ.
The force of that envy compels them to break their deep silence and to publish in words their hidden grief.
The fourth fierce beast has given us such offspring, whom she leads, armed, with her into hostile battles.

Here too join those whom bristling Caucasus fashioned from hard crags, those to whom savage Hyrcanian tigresses put their udders. Nourished on the milk of wild beasts, it is no wonder if they are wild in their ways and in their hearts.

You would sooner thrust Cacus down into his dark cave, and Alcides would sooner bear down from above with weapons on him, shut in the hollow rock and bellowing strange cries, and spend all his arms, pressing on with branches and huge millstones, than you could relieve this race of men of their stiff neck and lead them by warning into the right path.
The last race follows, more savage than the other troops: a race hard from its root, cruel, merciless and proud.

The boys stay awake to hunt and weary the woods. Their sport is to wheel horses and aim arrows from the bow, to carry off plunder swiftly and live on what they seize, to sever all right and wrong with the monstrous sword, to take no account of the eternal Deity, to speak with sacrilegious mouths and pour out impious words three times over. So they pass their lives and never remember the Thunderer.
If only it were permitted to see them, their minds pressed by wavering dread, and to look up to heaven from time to time!

sentences.en: Who is this striding before the front line, shouting things fit and unfit to be told? Is it Ulysses, the contriver of speech?

So do rocks roar when hurled from a siege engine, nor do such great crashes burst from a thunderbolt as the crashes roused by the dreadful voice of unspeakable crimes, crimes that demand the avenging right hand of the high Judge: the fierce punishments, I say, of the Judge upon the guilty, on account of the offended wrath of the Godhead.
1. Does not the very blood of innocent Abel, poured out at the altars, slain by his brother's murder, give voice?
There are those in recent times who have made a father see his son's death before his eyes, and have defiled a father's face with death.

How many has grievous ambition, how many has the dire lust for possessions, secretly overcome with the sword when they were off their guard? The flooding blood has sounded in the ears of Christ. 2. The oppression of the underage boy and of the widowed mother strikes the lofty heaven.
3. The all too foul overflow of the Sodomites' lust is known to the lands; where has a mournful song not re-echoed?
Would you deny that the walls of Jericho could be overturned by this terrible sound of the trumpet? What opposing force could resist?
In these thrice three ways we are held by another's stain: these are nine weapons. The right hand will hurl none of them against comrades in vain, without the horror of a wound falling upon them.

Would not Achitophel, had fate not been adverse to him, have prepared without delay to rout the Jessean camp with savage slaughter? Such resolute breasts would not have borne such spirits.

But what a woman can do with a mad command, and how fierce those weapons are to men, the Trojan hero learned well enough, tossed about so much on land and sea by the power of the gods, because of the unforgetting wrath of cruel Juno.

And to sing of sure things, known best to the whole world: when once, at God's command, the Baptist opens to the fates to come his lips, whose words the cruel king of the sons of Isaac sometimes believed, Herodias, that slippery woman, shows by the grim stroke of the blade what she can do with her command. By that stroke the light of the Christ-born race and its most faithful hope lies dead, the herald made outstanding by divine gift, refusing to prolong any further a life cut short.
But when the storm of Saul's harsh assent strikes, what bristling hail of stones does not come rattling down on the head of the innocent man? (Men of old called him Stephen.)

This man was distinguished for piety and gazed on the heights above. As Saul, thirsting in his heart for his death, harries him by the hands of two thousand of his followers, he also violates the man's right hand with a wound and overwhelms the holy man with a savage shower of hail.

But we are assailed by another bitter cast of a weapon. There are some whose pursuit it is, and whose heart's will moves them, to goad virtue with haughty words like these: 'You, a man? But how can I bear to say it? Why is your right hand cold in war? Is sloth what your heart likes? Does it please you always to gather fresh spoils and live on plunder?'

sentences.en: 'You have garments embroidered with saffron and gleaming purple, your tunics have sleeves, and your turbans have ribbons. O true Phrygian women, for you are not Phrygian men, go over the heights of Dindyma, where the pipe plays its two-holed song for those used to it. The timbrels and the Berecynthian luxury of the Idaean mother are calling you. Leave arms to men, and yield to the sword.'
With such words they burn to mock the gentle, goading them to dare worse through fierce Mars.

Should Wickedness stop, when she does not seem to have sharpened rabid furies enough with these things? With no gentle goads she stirs up anger. Having set about plying tricks and Pelasgian arts, she works to make glory give praise to vice, so that no one may refuse, for so great a hope, to attempt whichever of the six crimes the dread one holds out to the one who commits it.

But when she perceives that some are held by a heavier plague, she refuses to let them be betrayed or their hidden crime be uncovered. This is not, as is certain, to keep rumor from being able to oppose foul shame, or to keep the badly slippery darts of the tongue from piercing a good name and the iron from staying lodged in the breast. It is rather so that every wickedness may rule with loose reins, and the evil may creep further if it goes unpunished.

Busied also, by her indulgence, with the cares of the wicked, she strives by whatever means she can to stoop to every kind of entreaty, so as to avert the just wrath of the Judge, which neither human virtue nor piety itself could soften. Broken by God's command or by the fates, she scarcely falls silent.

So utterly without reason does the wicked mind rage, always closing its eyes and afraid to catch sight of the sun. Yet there is no more effective remedy for such troubles than for someone to cut open the top of the ulcer's mouth with a blade. The poison is nourished and lives by being concealed.
But the black night of crimes hovers all around with its hollow shade, unspeakably urging that the wicked deeds committed be defended, and asserting that this rightly seems to it no crime at all.

sentences.en: Would Wickedness not know how to accept a stolen share of a pilfered thing? Is it burdened by another's fraud?
My mind is foolish enough that I think I can succumb to my own fault. Depart far from here, you plagues of others! I must act, so that the foreign night of crimes does not dominate me.
Kindly Spirit, I ask you to direct our steps by your divine power, strengthening them when they falter with the strength of the virtues.

Behold, the noble phalanx of the Heavenly Ones sends itself into battle, with the Leaders of the virtues and the whole army of cavalry, arranged by number into squadrons. Over the whole plain the prancing steed roars and fights against the tightened reins, turning this way and that. Then far and wide the field bristles with iron spears, and the plains blaze with raised weapons.

Here, on the opposite side, the Cyprian leader, smooth-faced Cupid, appears on the plain facing them, together with his sister, Venus's ruinous Pleasure, and ill-counseling Hunger, and the frantic love of possessing, then fickle Ambition and Glory drenched in deceit, all of whom the Elation of an inflated mind joins as allies. Drawing back their right hands, they thrust their spears far forward and brandish their darts, and the advance of the men and the roaring of the horses grow fierce. And now each side had come within a spear's throw and halted. Suddenly they burst out with a shout, and in their fury urge on their horses. At once they pour thick volleys of weapons from every side, like snow, and the sky is covered in shadow.

sentences.en: At once, from the opposing camps, Chastity and Cupid charge at each other, straining with their spears. They are the first to deal ruin, with a mighty crash, and they smash the chests of their galloping steeds together, breast against breast, until they shatter. The adulterer is thrown off and hurled headlong far away, like a thunderbolt or a weight shot from a catapult, and scatters his life into the breezes. Chastity may lawfully risk this outcome of war only when she sees that she can no longer escape the fight by running, nor turn back the pressing Cytherean.

For a virgin who cultivates, undefiled, an eternal love of virginity would rather have prepared to turn her back, had she not been caught up in such warfare; but hostile force three times compelled her to take up arms in her hand.

Wicked Pleasure, unable to bear her brother's slaughter, began to turn over wiles in her mind and addressed Chastity with these words: "What is so remarkable if you, a woman, trust in a strong horse? Give up flight, trust yourself to face me hand to hand on level ground, and gird yourself for a battle on foot. Soon you will learn to whom windy glory brings praise."
"Plague," she says, "do you really think Chastity can be violated by fraud like this? Who would ask whether it is deceit or valor in an enemy?
You thunder with your mouth, though you are always readier to deceive. Go far away from here to turn over your wiles, carrying back ample spoils, you and your boy Cupid, with his face changed.
There is no virtue in settling the matter with you by the sword; it would sooner be an honor even to withdraw myself from the fight,
It is fear that proves minds degenerate, not an immense love of the virginal flower and of protecting snowy beauty.

I would dare to hand my horse over to a companion and stand in equal arms, on foot with a bare sword and undaunted with a plain shield, ready to clash with two thousand other Camillas. But with you, just reason forbids it. Rather, it wants wings bound to my feet, and the will stands firm in my heart to have won by flight.
Scarcely had she said this when, fleeing, she is carried off with her reins turned, and she wears out her swift steed with her iron spur. So the maiden is rescued from danger in safe warfare.

At once the battle lines are thrown into confusion. The guilty turn, throw their shields behind them and wheel their horses toward the walls. The stronger side pursues and drives its squadrons against the enemy.

sentences.en: And now they were approaching the gates when the fleeing ones again raise a shout and bend back their horses' supple necks. These flee and are carried far back with loosened reins.

It is just as when the sea rushes forward in alternating surges, foams, and drenches the farthest sand with its swell. Then it swiftly runs back, sucking in the rocks rolled back by its tide, and flees, leaving the shore as the shallows slip away.

Twice the just drove the routed guilty to the walls. Twice, driven back by arms, they look behind them, covering their backs. But when they met in the third battle, they entangled whole lines with one another, and man picked out man. Then indeed there were the groans of the dying, and in deep blood arms, bodies and half-dead horses were rolled together, mingled with the slaughter of men. A fierce battle arises.

Vain Superstition is slain. The false religion of the gods is dear to her; she was once accustomed to seal treaties over a slaughtered pig and, equipped with Stygian poisons, to arm the nation's prophetic seers for battle. Her head, struck off at close quarters by a single blow, lay far away with its helmet. The Ardor of Justice claimed this slaughter for itself, so that the distinguished glory of the deed would not be suppressed, with Christ as heavenly avenger.

But hoary Faith, who is the shield of the great Thunderer, catches the Sect of unspeakable heresy with its hamstring cut, and buried her dread sword up to the hilt in its back, for Christ supplies strength and courage. Then Disagreements fall, and Dissension, and the Rival right hand. Drunkenness collapses. Liber, who as victor bent the yokes with reins of vine shoots, driving his tigers down from the lofty peak of Nysa, felt that he had met an Achilles.

While Sobriety cleaves his forehead down the middle with the sword, between the twin temples, and at the same time his jaws with a huge wound, the earth was shaken by the huge weight. Dying, he strews on the ground his collapsed limbs and his arms bloody with brains, and his head hung in equal halves this way and that, over each shoulder.

sentences.en: When Zeal saw the ally of Venus and of impure Lyaeus laid low, Deceit withdrawing from the line, and the leaders thrown into confusion, he suddenly burns fervent with hope. He calls for his horses and his arms together, and with a proud leap springs into the chariot and works the reins with his hands. Flying about, he gives many brave bodies to death with his hand; he sends many rolling half-dead, or tramples the ranks with his chariot, or hurls seized spears at those who flee.

Just as when bloody Mars, roused beside the streams of icy Hebrus, clashes on his shield and, stirring up wars, lets loose his raging horses: they fly over the open plain faster than the South and West winds, and furthest Thrace groans, struck by their feet; and around him the faces of black Terror, and Wraths, and Ambushes, the god's retinue, are swept along.

Such is the eager victor in the midst of the battle, driving on his horses smoking with sweat and trampling the slain enemies, a pitiable sight: the swift hoof scatters bloody dews, and gore mixed with sand is trodden underfoot.

And now he has given Cypris to death, and three thousand monsters of foul crimes, to be roasted in the Stygian furnaces; and all those whom the madness for gold and the love of possessing tormented, he destroyed and plunged in bitter death. Ambition is laid low, and with her the Glory of vain praise; at this the limbs of the rest are loosened with cold, and life flees with a groan, indignant, down to the shades.

But although the forces of the hostile army are broken by this outpouring of war's strength, no peace will follow; for the plagues, despising the Deity, roar out such words as these: "Why should we no longer place our hope in our arms?"
Are we so deserted? Once our line has been turned, do we perish utterly? Has fortune no way back?
We have wealth, and youth still untouched, and various cities and peoples remain to help us."

But glory came to the party of the Gods above with much blood. They too have their own deaths, and the storm is the same for all. Why then do we falter, to our shame, on the very threshold? Why does trembling seize our limbs before the trumpet sounds?
Many a day, and the shifting labor of changeable time, has brought things back to a better state. Fortune, returning to many in turn, has mocked them and then set them once more on solid ground.

sentences.en: Let them therefore take up arms again. Suppose no peace follows, for such a peace would be too shameful. Can virtue be corrupted? Let her sooner seek arms and choose to clash in war, and let it come to her mind that it is beautiful to die in arms. Glory will always be subject to envy, and vice to shame. Will not the greatest part of the earth be a help to glory?

But Christ will be the great King of heavenly Olympus. Then, with the protection of the Gods above surrounding us, and the leaders whom so many peoples have sent, no small glory will follow those chosen from Latium and the Laurentian fields: few in number, but their valor vigorous in war.

It is right for everyone to undertake the sacred commands of the highest Father. It is not enough to have fled evil; the other part remains: to learn Justice and to extend virtue through deeds. For to know what is right and yet to walk a crooked path deserves double punishment, as the sacred Page explains, the sure interpreter of the great Thunderer.
What are you plotting? With what hope do you waste your leisure on vain things by delaying? Do you not regard the city granted by the fates?

Chosen race of men, offspring of the high blood of the gods, behold: it is perhaps granted to you to escape into the upper air by the rowing of wings. Bind to your feet the golden winged sandals, which may carry you aloft on wings over the seas or over the land, as swift as the rushing wind.

sentences.en: Just as the Cyllenian offspring, coming from his maternal grandfather, flew between the lands and the sky to the sandy shore of Libya and cut through the winds (as vain poets once imagined for us), so indeed you are able, relying on this threefold service of deeds, to enter the homes of heaven, to hold the high places above, and there to recline at the joyful tables of the gods.

Which by their merit have made the guilty worthy of heaven: may it please you to relieve the afflicted circumstances of the poor. And accustom yourself to pray to God with constant prayers, the author of the fruits of the earth and the ruler of storms. There is no need to try out approaches, or to look for the most favourable times for speaking, or the right way to handle the matter; He hears everyone so readily and so swiftly, ready to help the wretched. Do not let your faith waver, and persist in frequent prayer, for He will grant pardon to your prayers and let go of His anger.

Finally, let your greatest care be to calm the stirred-up waves of the flesh. By these three strict laws of fasting you calm the swelling seas of an afflicted heart, put to flight the gathered clouds, and bring back the sun of justice and clear weather to the mind.
There is no need for Triton to strain with great force to thrust the ships off the sharp rock: behold, He lifts them with His trident.

God Himself, rejoicing to ease the labours of men, both opens up the vast Syrtes and calms the sea; and so you will glide on light wheels over the tops of the waves, until virtue brings you to the shores of heaven.

But if you have so great a love of summoning virtue through deeds (for it is certain that virtue consists in practice and effort), it will be good here to recall Dardanian Anchises, known by fame above the heavens, a man distinguished for his piety.

While the horns of the moon fill themselves with light for the third time, behold, a stranger drags out his life in the woods, among the deserted lairs and dens of wild beasts, off the path and wandering. The branches give him a miserable sustenance of berries and stony cornel-cherries, and the plants feed him with their torn-up roots.

sentences.en: Out of the woods, I say, there comes forward the strange form of an unknown man, worn out by extreme emaciation and pitiable in his dress, and as a suppliant he stretches out his hands toward the shore. They look at him: dreadful filth, an untrimmed beard, his clothing fastened together with thorns, but in all else a Greek, and once sent to Troy in his country's arms. Pious Anchises himself, without much delay, gives the young man his right hand and strengthens his spirit with a ready pledge.

1. Piety restores and cherishes him in his exhausted state, and labours to bring back his strength with rich feasts; 2. nor does she deny repeated draughts to his thirsty mouth; 3. and she covers his stripped body with a new garment,

covering the bare fleeces. 4. She releases the captive from the cave of the prison. 5. She relieves the one consumed by disease, or by a heavier wasting, with skill, with her hand, and with the potent herbs of Phoebus.
6. She receives him as a guest. 7. When he dies, she lays him in the earth, offers funeral rites to the unknown man and honours him with a tomb.

Earth is heaped up into a mound, and altars to the Manes stand in mourning with dark blue fillets and black cypress, and around them stand the Trojan women with their hair unbound, as custom requires.
Do not be reluctant to say, gentlest of the Trojans, who taught you this kind of duty. Surely it was not a soldier of the Myrmidons, fierce in arms, or of the Dolopians, or of harsh Ulysses?

Such a man was always the destruction of his enemies, and it has never been found that he came to the aid of men who had dared to follow the opposing camp. But whatever belongs to the gentile lot, anywhere at all, delights in destroying the enemy with the sword.

It was therefore an outstanding piety, innate in you and not implanted by anyone's deeds, that made you spare the Greek enemy of your own accord, a piety I would praise to the skies. But our praise is too small to serve as thanks for so great a deed. Yet what glory of honour could touch you in your absence? It is nothing to be borne above the ether of heaven, and, in person, to have one's breast scorched by the flames of the Styx.

sentences.en: O race of Christians, born to better fates, to whom it is granted under the auspices of the divine Godhead to win the high seats of the heaven-dwellers and rewards far better than are truly owed to our merits: fired in mind by these things, do not yield to the profane race. Or would not an immense shame convict degenerate souls,

That you should be called Christians (you to whom, for so many years, the brave deeds of the Fathers have been known, a very long series of events handed down through so many men from the ancient origin of the race), and yet not have followed the illustrious examples of the Saints?
Let your one care be that of an excellent man: to kindle virtue by deeds. So the fates command; let no delay hold you back.
It is fitting not only to indulge the body's health; rather, Piety, born of God, thirsts to defend the so many wounded parts of the soul, and burns as she protects them.
1. This is her duty: to challenge the guilty with words and, look, to stir up harsh wars against wickedness with varied warnings.

Is it your heart's wish to build a road? But look, there are those who delay to call their step back from vices. Now that the sun has returned, the martial song of hoarse bronze sounds out here, and a voice is heard imitating the broken blasts of trumpets.

2. To illuminate ignorant minds and, once night has been put to flight, to instruct them in the excellent art of heavenly Pallas. 3. To take counsel, to weigh all the misfortunes of those who are afraid, and then to say which better opinion should stand firm in the mind.

6. Let neither grief nor the injury of a despised lot break you. Do not let wounded patience supply you with weapons, as frenzy does, lest you seem like those places where hollow rocks resound with a striking sound and the struck image of the voice bounces back.
7. Finally, she wants it to sit fixed and unmoved in your mind that you must not ponder any vengeance in an inflamed heart, overcoming the wrong with the strength of a tranquil heart.
In this way we shall be an ornament to Christ. Our fame will not be reported as slight, and the glory of so great a deed will grow.

sentences.en: Weighed down with heavy bronze, the fourfold hinge of heaven also creaks on its brazen doors. I mark it out in a twofold verse: the rule of Justice, Prudence, Strength from on high, and the power that lets loose upon things reins balanced with measure.
…will turn away from the right those troubled by a grievous wound of the mind; not even if it should pour the earth into the waves, mixing all in a deluge, or send heaven down into Tartarus.

Unless the monstrous gluttony of our palate soothes our mouths, parched with thirst, with the gushing streams of leaping water, and unless hunger is taken away and the love of eating restrained, measure will be lacking. But measure is the fairest virtue; without it virtue becomes vice and wounds modesty.

Since measure sets both the bounds and the times of things, hence that most famous poet rightly sang: there is a measure in things; there are, in short, fixed limits, beyond and short of which the right cannot stand.
Moreover, when the hinges of high heaven are torn away, what use are solid doorposts, and what use are brazen thresholds?

No way need be forced so that the door totters under repeated blows of the ram until the gate falls forward, its hinge wrenched out. The house within comes into view and the long halls lie open, from which the serpent of the Styx, hurled down by a thunderbolt to the shades, dragged great ruin with him from the world with a crash.

sentences.en: Do not, however, believe that the doors stood open against the will of the heavenly shores, so that violence has been done to the Thunderer. For the inner house, splendid with royal adornment, is thrown open so that, with destruction shut out from the high seats of the Winged Ones, it may be wholly free of the Stygian plague.

The palace does not need to be surrounded by battlements and a host, in the manner of a camp. Rather, the almighty Father has already hidden the terrors away in black caverns far from there: the tyrants of Cocytus, broken in adverse war.
Indignant, with a great murmur, they roar around the barriers of Avernus, but their angers are without strength, however great the Shades sent back from Acheron might be.

Meanwhile the greatest Michael, the lofty right hand of the Thunderer, and beside him Gabriel, the second hope of our race, lead the host and at the same time fill the places far and wide with soldiers. Both are outstanding in courage, both in surpassing arms, and wherever the enemies might clash with arms, they will beware of those arms.

Snatching your body from your bed, soon stretch your upturned hands to heaven along with your voice, and pour undefiled offerings upon the hearths. When the honor is completed, hasten joyfully to bear the pleasing work to the highest Thunderer. See to it that at the same time you adore the great Divinity of Mary with prayer.
With how much of Pallas' art has she made men distinguished, rejoicing to bring aid to the affairs of men!

Gladly sing her vows, and overcome the powerful mistress with suppliant vows. "O this band," she says, "O my chosen band, let no foreign band divert you from your undertaking, nor whatever monsters Erebus brings forth in its vast lakes and belches from the dire jaws of Orcus. For the King of the Gods above Himself breathes an impregnable vigor into His own, so that strength may stand solid in their breast, and He strengthens their minds and supplies them with weapons."
He strengthens the mind with the ethereal art of divine Pallas, instructing His children to look upon the high heavens and to decide their own affairs by the highest cause of things.

sentences.en: Increasing the powers of the intellect by the gift he bestows, heaping up the glory of counsel from heaven's lofty citadel, and sending forth from the sky the sublime gifts of Minerva; the gifts of heavenly strength, the distinguished paternal shield, and the veil woven round with saffron acanthus, the ornaments of divine piety; the gifts of the fear of the eternal Godhead. In short, what gifts would the royal offspring not bestow, with such great love for his mother?
These words the Virgin speaks briefly, her face cast down, so that from this you may easily see that nothing is more powerful than she at bending her Son by prayer and winning him over with a nod.
Gifts for the beloved race and for the flocks of her own people, for the bands chosen for their piety after the manner of a sodality.
Whoever the Spirit adorns with the sevenfold gift of the divine ones, He inflames with a wondrous love of the highest virtue.

Therefore, burning in spirit, he urges himself on. Matching every pattern of the virtues with mighty deeds, as though he had achieved nothing yet and the time for doing deeds were slipping away, he toils all the more and summons all his arms. Even now about to increase the honor of the heavenly ones, he shapes himself by zeal and practice to the manner of the heavenly ones.

At the same time joys thrill his mind, and He makes him be borne along ever tranquil in divine order, cherishing with abundant peace one who has been tossed by so many chances of life, and training him with a brave heart to endure all labors:
to hold out and keep himself for better fortunes; to relieve wretched men with signal piety; to check the waves of anger; and duly to receive a quiet spirit and a kindly mind toward his companions.

He grants that hearts which do not know how to bend should suddenly grow gentle, and with greater light He strengthens those who are unshaken in faith. Ordering the acts of the human body, He tempers them, and grants that they be modest in the manners of a lowly mind; that they preserve virginal grace and an outstanding pattern of snowy modesty, and keep a chaste bed.

sentences.en: If I am so selective about my horses that I spend special labor, from their tender years onward, on the ones I have decided to rear as the hope of the breed, and with all zeal keep off the ice and snowy winds, bring them oats, the most pleasing fodder, as food, and do not close the haylofts all winter long, how much better is the care that must be given to the salvation of the soul!

It is right to rouse sluggish minds, hearts unaccustomed to the study of sacred things and weary of the high Deity; it is right to rouse sluggish men by warning and men inert of mind with a resounding voice, and to kindle Mars with one's voice.
Or, because there is some grace in unplowed land, will you let the sluggish field harden with neglect?
Rest must be granted to perishable things, I concede (for what lacks all rest does not last), yet leisure must be fled, that Lerna of evils.

Hence there will be yellow Ceres, spelt under a changed name, in the place where you previously removed the legume gathered with its shaking pod, or the slender offspring of the vetch, and the fragile stalks and rustling forest of the bitter lupine.
For the labor is easy when crops alternate; only do not be ashamed to saturate the dry soils with rich dung, or to scatter foul ash over the exhausted fields.

The mind with its cheeks bathed in tears and suffused with shame, the avenging punishments of crimes, fasts added to whips, with groaning, and breasts beaten three times with fists, are to be likened to rich dung and to the farmers' ash, suited to the fields of the Gods, to whom heavenly things are a care:

sentences.en: And because, as I said, the fields rest when the crops are changed, you should bring there ample seeds (1) of rich praise; and where previously (2) slender vetches and bitter lupines, and indeed (3) burrs, caltrops and a bristling forest of vices used to come up, there let Gargara now marvel at harvests of virtues and of the sacred crop, now that the filth has been torn out from the lowest root. So may the mind in a sound body flourish through the long years of long-lived Nestor.

Some trouble the blind seas with their oars and rush onto the sword; they force their way into the courts and thresholds of kings. This one assails a city and its wretched homes with destruction, so that he may drink from a jewelled cup and sleep on Tyrian purple.

The royal offspring, on the other hand, spoke these words: Happy is he who has been able to despise the treasures of the rich, and who has cast beneath his feet all fears, inexorable fate, and the roar of bitter Acheron.

Neither the fasces of the people nor the purple of kings has swayed him. He has not been moved by discord driving faithless brothers, or by the Dacian descending from the conspiring Danube, or by the affairs of Rome and kingdoms doomed to perish. Nor has he either grieved in pity for the destitute or envied the one who has. He has plucked the fruits that the branches and the willing fields themselves have borne of their own accord, and he has never seen iron laws, the mad forum, or the people's archives. Rather, his will stands fixed in his mind to live in humble cottages and under the turf-heaped roof of a poor hut.

When the sun, hidden in a cloud, has mottled his rising dawn with spots and has shrunk back in the middle of his disk, be wary of showers. For the South wind, sinister to trees, crops and the flock, is pressing on from the deep.

sentences.en: Or when, toward dawn, scattered rays break forth among dense clouds, or when Aurora rises pale, leaving the saffron bed of Tithonus, then, alas, the vine-leaf will poorly shield the ripe grapes, so thick does the bristling hail leap crackling on the roofs. But the grapes of the heavenly vine, which the vine-leaf protects and to which heavenly gifts have given mild spirits, will not be gathered by the harsh hail, nor by the crueler breeze.

The savage madness of tyrants and the striking storm, the dire edge of iron and the burning desire to shed blood, the hostile force of men, and yet the insatiable heart bent on exercising hatred against the venerable name of Christ: all these are to be regarded as a pruning-hook, whose use the half-pruned, leafy vine on the elm needs for God. The work begun must be completed in this way. So, cultivated, the vine, very rich in Bacchus, will pour forth its wealth in full abundance, and the vintage is baked on the sunny rocks.

As many harvests as Gargara has, as many clusters as Methymna has, so many stony hearts of the harsh tyrant press the purple crops of the grape. The flood streams from the presses, and the foaming vintage overflows the brimming vats.

The victim that rises for Christ does not fall to die, for it is right for him now to rise again to the eternal realms of life. Nor will he have left the borders of his fatherland or its sweet fields, since his home is the hall of heaven and it is given to him to rejoice in a throne and the crown of a kingdom. These rewards, owed for his merits, are rendered to the Just man, whom mild hearts make serene. The gentle man is worthy not only to look upon the vaults of heaven, but also to hold his own sceptres on earth.

For just as a man with a fierce tongue inflames anger by what he says, so, on the other hand, a pious man calms the fires of anger with gentle speech. It is as when sedition has broken out in a great people, as often happens, and the base mob rages in their hearts: already torches and stones are flying, and madness supplies the weapons. Then, if they happen to catch sight of some man of weight, respected for his piety and merits, they fall silent and stand by with ears pricked up, and he rules their minds with his words and soothes their hearts.
Rightly, therefore, I shall declare gentle hearts fortunate for rule over both earth and heaven (but with Christ as guide).

sentences.en: Let the world, in its own way, mingling joys with empty cares, exult with applause and celebrate its own feasts.

Meanwhile, in the midst of the applause, death, the final line of life, is hastened on and soon draws near before the doors; and he is the first, before the day is done, before Evening closes Olympus and lays the day to rest, to bid these men fall by a swift doom.

Ah, how much better it would have been for them, if the fates had allowed it, to have dragged out their lives afflicted, in darkness and mourning through the years, and to have given themselves over to sorrowful grief for their sins, than, for so brief a time of gladness, to be condemned to eternal punishments and shut up in a dark prison.

O how happy are the souls in whose every vein a fiery thirst has been driven, a thirst that the fruit of justice cannot quench, and in whose minds an equal hunger has been implanted at the same time! Through this hunger the soul would wish its life poured out with all its blood. It would do so to extend the empire of Christ, and so that vain Superstition, which turns itself into so many faces, might depart defeated from its deceitful altars; that savage rites and fierce peoples might bow their necks to the pleasant yoke and, with the darkness driven away, behold the heavenly light; that the Roman Father might give laws through all lands; that the impious race might be rooted out of the whole world, and a golden race might grow throughout the whole world.

sentences.en: Enough now has this ardor been turning in our bones, Christ, enough. Will it never be right, great King, to seal your faith with blood? To what end such great desire, to what end this zeal in our souls, if everything comes to nothing and all our labor is lost? Look, we have not yet come to wounds here; we have stood in battle without bloodshed. We ask great things, we confess, undeserving as we are. Grant, O grant, that we may be able to merit what through you we are given to hope for. You are the author of the gift.

But how happy are those in whose soul the zeal to show mercy is firm and immovable! For, with the Supreme as witness, those who have tears, and whose minds are touched by mortal sorrows, are the ones Almighty God pities from high heaven.

When the image of Christ's pity comes to mind, Christ, whom, when he took pity on the fallen, this pity drove to undergo so many labors that, innocent, he laid down his life with all his blood, dying guiltless for the guilty, ah, with what cares did he groan, with what fires did he burn?
As this pity enters my mind, I am compelled by great flames to show mercy. Moved by the love of Christ, I am resolved in my mind to extend virtue by outstanding deeds.

The faith is made manifest by greater auspices: he whose soul's inner lights shine with divine power is deemed born under an exceedingly happy star. It is just as when the Morning Star, bathed in the Ocean's wave, whom Venus loves above the other fires of the stars, raises his sacred face to the sky and dispels the darkness. Clinging in his gaze, fixed upon the One among those above, he stands rejoicing until he is summoned by joyful Heaven.

Happy too are the minds which, with strife laid aside, have joined treaties of peace among companions. But souls take up victorious arms against the flesh and fight like boxers, both straining with all their strength, so that the flesh gives way and is laid low in the middle of the arena; and they are worthy both to be called and to be considered the sacred offspring of God.

marginalia.text: Musa Maronis, circa octauam Beatitudinem, suam ignorantiam agnoscit, cupitque à suo Ductore, etiamsi proprio Marte vti debeat, exactius institui.
marginalia.text_en: The Muse of Maro, concerning the eighth Beatitude, acknowledges her ignorance, and desires to be more exactly instructed by her Guide, even if he must use his own effort.
marginalia.explanation: The note explains the dramatic handover: the Muse admits that Virgil supplies no ready doctrinal answer and asks the catechetical speaker for instruction before composing more freely in her own words.
